articles.title_orig: Court denies request to halt execution of Texas man in wake of Christa Pike's botched lethal injection
articles.title_zh: Court denies request to halt execution of Texas man in wake of Christa Pike's botched lethal injection
articles.content_orig:
A Texas court on Wednesday refused to halt the execution of a man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk after his attorneys cited the failed lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee in a bid to stop the procedure.
The execution was scheduled to take place later Wednesday in Texas and would be the first in the U.S. since Pike survived the execution attempt last week.
Because Texas planned to inject the same drug used in Pike's attempted execution — pentobarbital — attorneys for 46-year-old Jamaal Howard argued to the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals that the drug poses similar risks. They also raised concerns about the quality of the state's execution drugs.
The court denied the request for a stay and later denied a second attempt to stop the execution over the drug. The court issued both denials without elaboration. The U.S. Supreme Court also denied a late appeal Wednesday evening without comment.
"Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee's footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys argued in their filing.
Pike's lawyers were seeking more information about what went wrong after the 50-year-old survived two doses of pentobarbital. She was hospitalized and, as of Tuesday, was awake and speaking .
In a statement Tuesday, her attorneys said she was "conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," but noted "her prognosis remains unclear" and "at a minimum," they "expect a long recovery."
They also said, "Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed."
One of her attorneys, Steve Ferrell, told "CBS Mornings" on Monday that doctors were working to clear her body of the pentobarbital and that she was on a ventilator.
Her attorneys have alleged her execution was marred by blown veins, where a needle goes all the way through a vein and causes a leak of blood and fluid, as well as Tennessee's deteriorated pentobarbital and a lack of emergency medical care.
"There is a similar risk," Howard's attorneys wrote, "that Texas's execution drugs are likewise degraded, as they are far past the original beyond-use dates that the pharmacopeia allows for drugs of this kind."
Texas has executed six people so far this year, with two more scheduled after Howard, which would be the 30th execution nationwide in 2026.
On Wednesday, Howard was described as "chatty" during the 45-mile drive from the death row prison to the Huntsville Unit where executions are carried out, said Amanda Hernandez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice.
"He made small talk with the officers through the whole trip," she said, adding he was taken to a small holding cell near the death chamber where he remained talkative.
"He was asking questions and was very engaged in the process," Hernandez said.
Howard was found guilty of capital murder in the 2000 killing of Vickie Swartout, 42, who was shot once in the chest during a robbery. Evidence presented at the trial included the store's surveillance video, which showed Howard shooting Swartout.
Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store in the small, rural town of Silsbee, located about 100 miles northeast of Houston, according to court records.
His attorneys have argued Howard is intellectually disabled and his execution should be halted. The state said he has not presented evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability.
He has an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court pending to stop the execution.
The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people. But it has given states some discretion in how they determine such disabilities.
The motion filed in the Court of Criminal Appeals in Texas early Wednesday said Howard's attorneys had filed requests for information about the lethal dose of pentobarbital the Texas Department of Criminal Justice planned to use. They say the department asked for a state attorney general opinion about whether they would have to disclose that information, despite a "years-long practice of disclosing information."
The Texas attorney general opinion is not expected to be returned until after Wednesday, meaning Howard can't litigate whatever decision the state might make on releasing that information, they say.
Texas officials did not immediately return a request for comment Wednesday morning.
Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method.
Tennessee's Republican Gov. Bill Lee has halted the one remaining execution for the rest of the year.
An execution date for former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan , who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, has been set for Dec. 3, and will take place at the same post where he carried out his attack, according to an email sent to the families of victims.
Hasan is set to die by firing squad in what will be the first military execution since 1961. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said late Monday the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and approved by President Trump.

articles.title_orig: EU-China trade talks begin in Beijing amid escalating pressure
articles.title_zh: EU-China trade talks begin in Beijing amid escalating pressure
articles.content_orig:
European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic has arrived in Beijing for talks on the European Union’s (EU) growing trade deficit with China.
Sefcovic will meet Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao on Thursday and Friday after months of discussions over the EU’s trade deficit of more than €1bn ($1.12bn) daily, as well as Chinese curbs on exports of rare earths and other critical minerals.
Meanwhile, Chinese companies are increasingly challenging Europe’s top car brands. China rejected the EU request for voluntary curbs on Chinese hybrid car exports as the two sides enter negotiations, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. The European Commission now hopes to get Beijing to accept a unilateral EU measure to cap hybrid imports instead, the outlet said, citing two diplomats briefed on the plan.
The two days of discussions come just as a majority of EU lawmakers called for a more assertive trade policy towards Beijing in a non-binding resolution on Wednesday. China vowed a “resolute response” to safeguard its industries if the European Union goes ahead with restrictions against Chinese companies or products, according to its commerce ministry.
French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, leaders of the bloc’s two biggest powers, on Tuesday urged the EU to prepare a “credible instrument” that could be quickly activated to strike back against countries that harm the bloc economically.
The new measure would not target any specific country. German officials said the EU needed a tool as powerful as the Section 301 tariffs imposed by the United States or China’s restrictions on critical-mineral exports.
The proposed weapon – to be discussed at an EU leaders’ summit next week – would give the European Commission the power to respond to a trade aggression within days.
China responded to the letter by urging Paris and Berlin to steer clear of “protectionist” measures.
“We hope that France and Germany, as major economies in the world, will uphold openness, cooperation and free trade,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.
“They should avoid going down the wrong path in the wrong way, only to ultimately suffer the consequences themselves.”
G20 finance leaders, except China’s, agreed in September to act against “non-market” distortions that exacerbate imbalances. Beijing says that hyping up issues such as economic imbalances and overcapacity is a form of protectionism designed to exert pressure on and restrict China.
EU and Chinese officials have been discussing trade imbalances since June. Sefcovic said he wanted “tangible results by October” as well as some form of commitment that can be put to EU leaders meeting in Brussels.
Trade relations with China top the summit’s agenda next week, as ballooning debt has prompted auditors to warn about the next seven-year EU budget and has spurred protests in France.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament last month that the trade imbalance had reached a tipping point and that Europe would use every tool at its disposal to rebalance the relationship.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike 'angry and confused' about Tennessee's failed execution effort, lawyers say
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike 'angry and confused' about Tennessee's failed execution effort, lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike began speaking a day after her legal team understood that life support would be withdrawn, her lawyer has said.
The Tennessee death row prisoner, 50, regained consciousness on October 6, almost a week after surviving an attempted execution by lethal injection.
Speaking outside a Nashville courthouse on October 7, attorney Randy Spivey said he had understood the previous evening that Christa was brain dead.
"But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone, Christa woke up and began talking," he said.
Frank Strada, the head of the Tennessee Department of Corrections, resigned on Saturday following the botched execution of Christa Pike (@ Alamy Live News.)
Randy said he had been told that Christa's first questions after waking included: "Where am I?"
He explained that he was not present when she regained consciousness. According to his account, she is aware of the execution attempt but remains confused about aspects of what happened.
Christa continues to face significant health problems, including pneumonia, a blood clot and difficulty swallowing, her legal team said. Her lawyers had announced her return to consciousness in a statement on October 6, while emphasising that her prognosis remained uncertain.
They also reported serious injuries to her arms and said she remained restrained in her hospital bed while receiving critical care. Those details were attributed to the legal team and had not been independently verified by local broadcaster WZTV.
The description of Christa as brain dead comes from her lawyer's account of what he understood. The reporting does not establish that doctors completed a formal brain-death determination.
That distinction matters. According to the American Academy of Neurology , brain death means the complete and permanent loss of brain function following catastrophic injury. It is different from a coma.
Cleveland Clinic explains that people do not recover from brain death. Medical guidelines also require clinicians to exclude factors, including the effects of sedating drugs, that could interfere with an assessment.
Christa's reported return to consciousness should therefore not be described as recovery from confirmed brain death.
A federal appeals court Wednesday morning halted the execution of Christa Pike, 50, who was 18 when she murdered a classmate (@ Alamy Live News.)
Tennessee attempted to execute Christa on September 30 at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution. Associated Press journalists who witnessed the procedure reported that she continued breathing after two injections and complained that her arm hurt. She was subsequently taken to hospital.
Frank Strada, the head of the Tennessee Department of Corrections, resigned on Saturday following the botched execution.
Christa was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student. Christa was 18 when she committed the crime and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Bill Lee, Governor of Tennessee (@ Sony Pictures via Getty Images)
At the October 7 hearing, Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered prison officials to preserve evidence connected to the failed execution.
"Anything in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," she said.
The order covers materials including medical equipment, records and communications. The judge also directed officials to respond promptly to requests from Pike's lawyers to visit her.
The Tennessee Attorney General's Office argued that a court order was unnecessary because evidence had already been collected and logged.
Governor Bill Lee has ordered an external review and postponed the state's other execution scheduled for this year. Investigators have yet to establish publicly exactly what went wrong.
Christa's longer-term medical outlook remains uncertain, and no decision on another execution attempt was announced at the hearing.
Assistant Attorney General John Ayers said the question of whether and when to set a new execution date would be for the Tennessee Supreme Court. Christa remains in hospital while her lawyers seek access to the evidence surrounding the September 30 procedure.

articles.title_orig: World leader in livestock fertility research closes out 58-year career
articles.title_zh: World leader in livestock fertility research closes out 58-year career
articles.content_orig:
After 58 years, Fuller Bazer, Ph.D., a University Distinguished Professor in the Texas A&M College of Agriculture and Life Sciences Department of Animal Science , will close out his scientific career in October.
During his groundbreaking tenure, Bazer also held joint appointments in the College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences Departments of Veterinary Integrative Biosciences and Veterinary Physiology and Pharmacology ,
“Dr. Bazer has built an enduring legacy as one of the foremost reproductive scientists in the world,” said Clay Mathis, Ph.D., head of the Department of Animal Science, “Dr. Bazer may be retiring, but his innovative work that transformed our understanding of pregnancy establishment in livestock will continue to have an impact on the industry for many years to come.”
Bazer is a Regents Fellow, Distinguished Professor, Presidential Impact Fellow, and the O.D. Butler Chair in Physiology of Reproduction, as well as a top researcher in the world in the “Animal Science and Veterinary” category, as named by Research.com .
At 88, he is ranked, according to Google Scholar, as the most highly cited researcher in the field of reproductive biology. He is credited with discovering uteroferrin, a phosphatase, produced in response to progesterone that transfers iron to the developing embryo and stimulates red blood cell development. He also identified estradiol as the pregnancy recognition signal in swine and interferon tau as the signal in ruminants — findings that have reshaped animal management practices to improve pregnancy outcomes.
Those findings were published across 58 years, from 1968 to 2025, averaging 16.9 papers a year, with 46 of the 982 publications appearing in the last two years.
Bazer earned his bachelor’s in biology from Centenary College of Louisiana, his master’s in animal science from Louisiana State University and his doctorate in animal science from North Carolina State University. He was a member of the Department of Animal Science, University of Florida from October 1968 to 1992 before joining the Texas A&M Department of Animal Science on May 1, 1992.
In addition to maintaining highly productive research and teaching programs, Bazer served as director of the Center for Animal Biotechnology and Genomics, 1992–2001; director of the Institute of Biosciences and Technology, Texas A&M University and Texas A&M Health Sciences Center, Texas Medical Center, Houston, 1994-2001; the inaugural vice president for research and interim dean of the Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, January 1999 to December 2000, Texas A&M University System Health Science Center.
He also served as the associate vice chancellor and associate director of the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station, and executive associate dean of the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, January  2001 to December  2004; associate vice president for research, January 2005–December 2008; interim department head, Department of Veterinary Pathobiology, May-February 2010; and the World Class University Professor, Biomodulation Major, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea, March 1, 2010 to Aug. 31, 2013.
Bazer has had an outstanding career and significant impact on livestock fertility and reproduction, signified by his recognition as the recipient of the 2003 Wolf Prize in Agriculture for his interferon tau discovery as well as his discovery of other pregnancy-associated proteins. Additionally, he received the Alexander von Humboldt Award in Research in 2000. These are two of the highest awards in the field of agricultural sciences.
Bazer is also past recipient of the highest awards from each of his scientific societies: the Carl Hartman Award from the Society for the Study of Reproduction in 2004, the Morrison Award from the American Society of Animal Science in 2014, and the Marshall Medal from the Society for Reproduction and Fertility in 2025. He is also a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and a recipient of the L.E. Casida Award for Graduate Education and the Animal Physiology and Endocrinology Award, both from the American Society of Animal Science. He earned awards for research, graduate education and service from the Society for the Study of Reproduction.

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Investigates Wells Fargo for Race-Based Lending
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Investigates Wells Fargo for Race-Based Lending
articles.content_orig:
This story was originally published on Bisnow, the newsroom global commercial real estate reads first. To receive daily news and analysis, subscribe to Bisnow's free suite of newsletters .
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development is initiating an investigation into Wells Fargo's mortgage lending efforts over commitments the bank made to bolster Black homeownership for nearly a decade.
Credit: Wikimedia Commons/Tdorante10
HUD sent Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf a letter Wednesday saying federal officials would probe whether the bank violated the Fair Housing Act through its attempts to boost minority homeownership.
The bank has made multiple attempts to aid Black homeowners in recent years.
In 2017, Wells Fargo announced that it would commit $60B in loans to add at least 250,000 Black homeowners by 2027, according to The Wall Street Journal . In 2022, it unveiled a $210M effort to expand racial equity in residential lending following a Bloomberg investigation that found the bank approved Black homeowners applying to refinance at a significantly lower rate than white homeowners.
A Wells Fargo spokesperson declined to comment on the investigation.
HUD alleges that by 2022, the bank "fully embraced sorting homeowners" and offering different products or terms based on race, wrote Craig Trainor, assistant secretary for fair housing and equal opportunity at HUD.
"Although Wells Fargo scrubbed its website of "DEI" references in 2025, the bank's obligations under the Fair Housing Act rise or fall based on actual practices, not buzzwords or website aesthetics," Trainor wrote in the letter.
Wells Fargo has walked back other diversity, equity and inclusion practices over the past couple of years, scrapping a policy in 2025 that had mandated diverse candidate pools for senior-level roles.
Trainor wrote that the bank's public statements, commitments and reports call into question whether it continues to make loans and craft terms based on the race of the applicant.
The investigation reflects the persistent pressure the Trump administration has put on companies to stand down from DEI practices, which has affected how CRE companies do business.
Landlords stand to risk losing federal leases if they're found in violation of anti-DEI policies. Commercial real estate companies have wiped DEI language from their websites. And CRE C-suites became less diverse in 2026 after five years of gains.

articles.title_orig: World of Warcraft: Forever Class Deep Dives — Rogue and Warlock
articles.title_zh: World of Warcraft: Forever Class Deep Dives — Rogue and Warlock
articles.content_orig:
Masters of subtlety and destructive power take center stage in this World of Warcraft: Forever class deep dive. Discover how Rogues and Warlocks are evolving through updates that build on the defining tools, tactics, and playstyles of each class.
For Rogues, the update builds on their mastery of Stealth, control, Poisons, and precise weapon attacks. Poisons gain more charges and can be used alongside temporary weapon enchantments, while updates across Assassination, Combat, and Subtlety create stronger options for daggers, other weapon types, Finishing Moves, Bleeds, and combat tricks.
For Warlocks, the focus is on opening new ways to command Shadow, Fire, and demonic power. Banes separate damaging effects from utility Curses, pets scale with their master’s stats, and revised Firestones and Spellstones strengthen spell-focused weapon imbues. Talent updates across Affliction, Demonology, and Destruction further support damage-over-time and draining effects, deeper demon synergies, and distinct Shadow and Fire combinations.
Talents become available starting at level 10 and continue using a familiar structure, including one-point milestone talents at 11, 21, and 31 points, now joined by a new 16-point milestone. To change your talents, including Legacy talents, visit a class trainer in one of the major cities. Dual Specialization also becomes available at level 40.
Please note that class abilities and talents may continue to evolve throughout the beta test and are subject to additional changes.
Rogues excel at creating opportunities and turning them into decisive advantages. These updates give them more ways to prepare for an encounter, adapt once combat begins, and shape a build around the methods that suit them best.
Removed talents : Dagger Specializaton , Mace Specialization , Sword Specialization , Fist Weapon Specialization have all been subsumed into the new talent Hack and Slash.
Removed talents : Sleight of Hand, Deadliness.
Rogues remain the masters of Stealth , with unique abilities useable from Stealth like Pickpocket , Distract , Sap , and Garrote . They alone have access to Poisons and can now use them alongside temporary weapon enchantments. However, different varieties of Rogues specialize in different weapons and tactics. Assassination specializes in daggers and buffing themselves with Finishing moves.  Combat and Subtlety have support for all weapon types, with Combat focusing on hard hitting direct damage and little bit of cleave damage with Blade Flurry , and Subtlety focusing on combat tricks and Bleeds. Whichever specialization they choose, Rogues are welcome in any party or raid for their Stealth and control abilities, as well as the highest potential single-target melee damage in the game.
Warlocks bend forbidden powers to their will, turning every resource—from lingering afflictions to bound demons—into another means of defeating their enemies. These updates broaden how they manage those powers and create new connections among their spells, pets, and specialized tools.
Removed talents: Improved Curse of Weakness, Improved Drain Life, Improved Drain Mana, Improved Curse of Exhaustion, Grim Reach, Dark Pact.
Removed talents : Improved Healthstone, Fel Intellect, Fel Stamina, Improved Subjugate Demon, Improved Firestone, Improved Spellstone.
Removed talents :  Improved Firebolt, Improved Lash of Pain, Devastation, Improved Immolate, Emberstorm.
Warlocks are gaining new exciting combat options for WoW: Forever. With Affliction, they can concentrate on damage-over-time and draining effects, now with full viability from dealing critical strikes and competitive damage, and with the ability to sustain their own health via powerful health draining effects. With Demonology, they can specialize in empowering themselves and their pet in all new ways with Demonic Brand , Demonic Knowledge , and Demonic Pact , keeping foes focused on their pet while they decimate the enemy with Soul Fire . And with Destruction, they can now mix powerful Shadowburns and Conflagrates with the new Incinerate spell, and the new Bane of Havoc allowing them to continue damage on a primary target while dealing with lesser foes. Warlocks are still physically weak themselves, depending on their demon pets for protection, but they now do damage to compete with any other spellcaster, with three completely different styles to conduct that competition.
Whether striking from the shadows or wielding forbidden power, Rogues and Warlocks offer distinct ways to approach every encounter. Explore their updated talents, experiment with new combinations, and find the tactics that best suit your path through World of Warcraft: Forever .

articles.title_orig: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.title_zh: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.content_orig:
‘Transparent information sharing’ from Moscow is required to conduct full risk assessment, UN agency says
The World Health Organization has said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia following the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia.
Darya Shipilova died two days after falling ill with cold-like symptoms . She was an employee at the anti-plague research institute in the eastern city of Irkutsk, with some reports suggesting she was infected after a workplace accident.
The Russian authorities have denied a connection with the institute and say Shipilova died from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology” . They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable.
At the same time, officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted.
On Wednesday the WHO director general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event and we’re not able to conduct a full risk assessment.
“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.”
Tedros said he also wanted more clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed media reports of “a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”.
“We assess any reporting from the community,” he said. “We asked Russia to respond to that. We’re waiting for an answer.”
The WHO’s director of epidemic and pandemic management, Maria Van Kerkhove, said the agency still did not know how Shipilova became infected in the first place – and with what viral disease. If pneumonic plague was ruled out, “what did she actually die from?” Kerkhove asked.
In an interview with local media , Shipilova’s 64-year-old mother, Svetlana, discounted the theory that her daughter had been infected after smashing a test tube. “I know the truth. I’m fending off stupid friends who believe this. A test tube is unbreakable, even if you throw it against the wall,” she said.
She described her daughter as a dedicated worker and “pure person” devoted to her job.
Former classmates are also sceptical she was infected at her workplace. One reportedly said: “They’ve smeared a woman without properly investigating. Knowing how hard-working and responsible she was, it just doesn’t add up for me.”
The Kremlin has sought to downplay the incident and has brushed aside an offer of assistance made earlier this week by Donald Trump, the US president. The White House has pressed Moscow for more details of the case, while stressing the risk to the US is very low.
On Tuesday Trump said he would speak about the plague issue “very soon” with Vladimir Putin, who celebrated his 74th birthday on Wednesday. The Kremlin said no call had been arranged but could be quickly organised.
According to the Baikal Medical Journal , health officials in Irkutsk have taken extensive measures to stop a potential outbreak from spreading. Neighbours said workers in white protective suits and gas masks disinfected the two-storey brick building where Shipilova lived several times after her death last Friday.
“The smell was unbearable and very pungent,” a woman in her 40s said. “A woman knocked on our door. I said: ‘What are you treating here?’ I already knew about the plague rumours.
“She said: ‘It’s for cockroaches.’ But we don’t even have any cockroaches in our building. I saw her packing her overalls into a bag. I was like, ‘Well, I get it.’”

articles.title_orig: World Girls Hockey Weekend comes to Carbondale
articles.title_zh: World Girls Hockey Weekend comes to Carbondale
articles.content_orig:
psullivan@postindependent.com
For the first time, World Girls Hockey Weekend is coming to the Roaring Fork Valley, giving girls and women a chance to hit the ice in Carbondale with no registration, fees or equipment required.
Colorado Extreme, a nonprofit dedicated to expanding hockey access in the Roaring Fork Valley, will host the free event at 5 p.m. Oct. 17 at the Steadman Philippon Outdoor Arena in Carbondale.
The event invites women of all ages in the Roaring Fork Valley, whether a seasoned skater or completely new to the sport, to come together and celebrate women’s hockey.
Colorado Extreme will provide free equipment to those who need it. Participants can bring a stick and play with friends, practice their skills or simply learn how to skate.
In addition to the free skate, Colorado Extreme will host a watch party with pizza for professional women’s hockey games.
No registration is required for the event.
World Girls Hockey Weekend is a global event that began in 2011. This year marks the first time the event has come to the Roaring Fork Valley as Colorado Extreme continues its mission to expand hockey opportunities for girls in the region.
“The biggest thing is just we’re trying to grow the girls’ game,” said Maddy Moses, a high-performance coach at Colorado Extreme.
Moses grew up playing hockey on the East Coast, where she said girls-only hockey programs were much more common.
“I grew up on the East Coast, so girls’ hockey is extremely prominent, and there’s so many opportunities,” Moses said. “That’s just not the case out west, and I feel like Colorado is getting on board with that finally, and giving girls opportunities to learn to play and to skate and to do it together, rather than just being a handful of girls on a boys’ team.”
Colorado Extreme has made accessibility a central part of its efforts to introduce more girls to the sport.
“It’s a really great place for young athletes that haven’t maybe experienced the sport to come to specifically Colorado Extreme and just try it,” Moses said. “I mean, it’s pretty unheard of that you go somewhere and you get completely free equipment and you get to get on the ice and you get to try it on multiple occasions.”
That same approach will carry into World Girls Hockey Weekend.
“No registration, no fees, nothing. Just show up. If you have gear, bring it. If you don’t have gear, we can get you some gear and get you out on the ice,” Moses said.

articles.title_zh: Much of the world sees tragedy in Gaza. Many Israelis, scarred by Oct. 7, see only a threat
articles.content_orig:
SDEROT, Israel — One by one, Israelis peered through the tourist-style binoculars at the shattered Gaza town of Beit Hanoun, a distance of several football fields away, where buildings tilted in the rubble like broken teeth. The only noticeable movement was dust kicked up by Israel’s military.
The Israelis squinted for a few moments and gestured others over. The lookout is a rare place where they can confront the Palestinian territory firsthand, and some celebrate its devastation.
An Israeli documentary released this year included one onlooker exclaiming, “Wow, destroyed beautifully.” The Associated Press heard similar sentiments there.
On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people in southern Israel and abducted 251 others, leading to a devastating war and, eventually, a fragile ceasefire.
Three years on, a visit to the communities attacked that day made clear: It’s too soon for many residents to see the Palestinians next door as anything other than a threat.
The highway running parallel to Gaza, where militants gunned down people trying to flee, is dotted with memorials. Victims’ smashed and bullet-pocked cars are assembled elsewhere, rusting and piled a half-dozen high. Portraits of young female military spotters, whose warnings about a potential attack were disregarded, mark their deaths that day.
One resident, Deganit Bar Hay, said she still can’t barbecue because the smell of burnt flesh — “the smell of hell” — is a trigger.
Globally, there is shock and condemnation over how Israel has conducted the war, and how Gaza remains in ruins and cut off from the world a year since the ceasefire. Over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, and the vast majority of its 2 million residents live in rat-infested tent camps or among the debris.
But empathy for them is still unthinkable for many in Israel, with memories raw. Israeli media report little on the Palestinians of Gaza, and Israelis rarely if ever hear their voices unless they seek them out.
A new Israeli documentary, “NAZA,” in which military insiders describe what they said was the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, has sparked outrage at the filmmakers, not the government. Everywhere in Israel — at train stations, beaches, the Gaza viewpoint — are dozens of stickers in memory of the hundreds of soldiers killed on Oct. 7 and in the ensuing war.
“We are post-traumatic, all of us,” said Ziporah Livneh, outside a cafe catering to tour groups and soldiers a short drive from Gaza. Much of her family died in the Holocaust, and she came to Israel at the age of 2.
Now, she said, the answer for Gaza is to keep believing in people’s humanity but respond strongly to acts of evil. A society and a country can’t be built on revenge, but for the world to think “we can be Mother Teresa, it is a hypocrisy.”
Many Israelis are still turned inward. They say their story isn’t being heard or understood. They assert that Palestinians in Gaza receive more attention, even as Israel’s government still prevents journalists from entering the territory except under rare, highly managed visits — and very few Palestinians can leave.
From the day the war began, Israeli news and hearts were focused on the dead and the hostages taken into Gaza, a land that despite being an hour’s drive from Tel Aviv has long felt remote. Cross-border contact had been severely limited since Hamas seized power in 2007. Then, on Oct. 7, militants ripped the fence apart.
This is the first anniversary since the attack that all remaining hostages are out of Gaza, alive or dead.
There is rebuilding in the Israeli communities where militants went home to home, burning and shooting. There is also the insistence on keeping Oct. 7 memories alive, with hope that the outside world will come to understand how Israel’s sense of security was smashed.
“I know many people around the globe don’t understand us,” said Mor Izreal, director of an Oct. 7 virtual reality exhibit in the border city of Sderot. She said over 10,000 people have visited since it opened a year and a half ago, most from overseas. Reactions range from sadness to rage to connectedness, she said.
This year, for the first time since the attack, there is also an election, a momentous and angry one.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is deeply divisive. Many Israelis accuse him of failing to prevent the Oct. 7 attack and not securing the hostages’ release sooner, before many of them were killed. He is also accused of corruption and threatening democratic institutions.
But there has been little criticism of how his government has treated the Palestinians in Gaza, where Israel’s military now controls over 60% of the territory, squeezing them into an ever-smaller space.
Next to a bullet-pocked rocket shelter outside Sderot, a man held a banner calling for an official inquiry into the security failures surrounding the attack. Netanyahu has long resisted one.
Amit Gurfinkel said he spent Oct. 7 in a safe room with his daughter in the nearby community of Netivot, holding a knife and expecting the worst.
Gurfinkel is a minority in a population that has long supported Netanyahu. Posted across Sderot are campaign banners for his far-right allies, Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir — the national security minister who has called for killing “30 to 40” people in targeted assassinations in Gaza each night.
Security is paramount, especially in Sderot, where residents have just 10 seconds to seek shelter when rockets are fired from Gaza. But Gurfinkel sees Israel’s reputation as crucial, too. He shook his head over passing drivers who shouted their support for Netanyahu, whose government is isolated over the destruction in Gaza and who has been issued an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court.
“This is pathological. I don’t know,” Gurfinkel said. “Sociologists and psychologists will have answers in the years to come.”
Some Israelis argue there are no real civilians among Palestinians in Gaza, pointing to Hamas’ entrenchment. Some Palestinians feel the same way about Israelis, noting that military service is mandatory for most Jewish men and women.
“Death to Arabs” is written inside a rocket shelter across from the Sderot police station that was besieged and then destroyed. “Hamas is still in Gaza” is scrawled on a guardrail on the highway where bodies spilled from vehicles on Oct. 7. “Make Gaza Jewish Again” is on a banner in a public square in Jerusalem’s Old City.
There is little public discussion about how everyday Palestinians are doing after three years of war.
“I think about them, and it’s complicated,” Adi Marmelstain said of the people in Gaza. She was visiting the sprawling memorial for the Nova music festival, where hundreds of people were shot dead on Oct. 7.
Her 20-year-old daughter, a member of the security forces like many young Israelis, stood in shorts and a tank top, her rifle slung across her. Both knew people who had been killed.
Marmelstain recalled waking up another daughter on Oct. 7 and sending her to war with bottled water and cookies. She later asked herself what she had been thinking. Three years later, life is not much easier to contemplate.
The world doesn’t see Israel in the right light, she said. And the Palestinians in Gaza?
“I think they have the right to live, but they choose not to,” she said.
Associated Press video journalist Alon Bernstein in Sderot, Israel, contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.title_zh: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.content_orig:
Chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in Antarctica down by two-thirds since 2011, probably due to climate crisis
The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed.
Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica , increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, Prof Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey .
The Guardian revealed in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem.
The new study, published on Wednesday in Current Biology, indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird – which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek – may need to be classified as an endangered species.
The island of Zavodovski had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic peninsula to 5C above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4C, about 20C above normal for the time of year – a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy”.
Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the north-west of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30% – though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.
after newsletter promotion
He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”
The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.
Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “Penguin Pompeii hypothesis” of a sudden population fall , this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.

articles.title_orig: Lamers Dairy wins awards at 2026 World Dairy Expo
articles.title_zh: Lamers Dairy wins awards at 2026 World Dairy Expo
articles.content_orig:
APPLETON, Wis. (WBAY) — Lamers Dairy in Appleton is celebrating two first-place awards at the 2026 World Dairy Expo.
The company won first place for its whole chocolate milk and its one percent low fat chocolate milk.
The annual competition evaluates products in all dairy categories. More than 1,200 entries were submitted by more than 150 companies.
Eric McGuire, vice president of Lamers Dairy, said the award is an honor.
“Every year that we can compete and win an award is certainly an honor,” McGuire said. “And it’s a testament to the, I think, the meticulous care and dedication that our colleagues and our farm patrons put into their work every single day.”
Lamers Dairy also won a second-place award for its half and half.

articles.title_zh: The Richest Man in the World Needs More Money
articles.content_orig:

Apparently, Elon Musk's SpaceX, valued at $2.2 trillion and led by a CEO worth $1 trillion, needs even more money.
The Financial Times reported late Tuesday that the rocket company is seeking $40 billion to buy more chips from its longtime partner and AI confidant, Nvidia.
"We've decided to build exclusively on Nvidia because we think the Vera Rubin architecture is the best architecture," Musk said in August.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Musk have a history of praising each other. On the BG2 Pod in October 2024, Huang called Musk the "ultimate GPU."
"He has a great sense of urgency and a real desire to build it. When will comes together with skill, unbelievable things can happen," he added.
One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.
SpaceX is seeking $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt, or corporate bonds rated BBB- or Baa3 and above, the safer tier of company debt. With the company rated Baa1 by Moody's and BBB by S&P Global Ratings, Apollo has plenty of options as it leads the financing and helps sell the debt to everyone from pension funds and life insurers to regulated financial institutions.
Wall Street didn't love the prospect of the company more than doubling its debt load, which stands at about $30 billion, according to companiesmarketcap.com . Shares of SpaceX (SPCX) are down 2.4% today. Its total debt-to-equity ratio is 0.31x, below the sector average. Boeing sits at the extreme, with a 10.0x D/E ratio, while Rocket Lab (RKLB) is around 0.61x.
Nvidia, on the other hand, got plenty of affection from Wall Street. News that Musk planned to buy exclusively from the AI-chip company sent its stock to another all-time high of almost $240 before it turned lower near the close. Nvidia is trading at $236 today.
But not everyone is as bullish on Elon's debt, the FT reports. Investors previously approached by the company received only a "short two-page deal memo" with "pictures of outer space" and "an arrow pointing out that the company was going to build data centers 'somewhere in the universe.'"
Given that the same company approved Musk's compensation package on the condition that he build a Mars colony with a permanent population of at least 1 million, and no deadline, this checks out.

articles.title_orig: Lone Jack teen Jax Cromwell carries US flag at Beach Wrestling World Championships
articles.title_zh: Lone Jack teen Jax Cromwell carries US flag at Beach Wrestling World Championships
articles.content_orig:
LONE JACK, Mo. — KSHB 41 reporter Tod Palmer covers sports business and eastern Jackson County, including Independence. Share your story idea with Tod .
Lone Jack isn’t anywhere near a beach, but that didn’t stop Jax Cromwell, a 2025 Mules graduate , from becoming a rising star for USA Wrestling’s Beach Wrestling Team during the last year, giving him a chance to see the world.
"One of my biggest dreams actually is to travel the world, so to do it through the sport I love is just amazing," Cromwell said.
Cromwell, 19, competed last month at the 2026 Beach Wrestling World Championships in Katerini, Greece, where he was chosen as the U.S. team's flag bearer.
He competes in the USA Beach Wrestling 90+ kilogram division, both as a U-20 athlete and in regular events.
“Never in a million years would I think a kid from a small town in Missouri would ever be able to get to do something like that, so I'm definitely blessed and honored to be able to represent our country in that way,” Cromwell said. “... It was just an amazing honor.”
While Lone Jack is a long way from the beach, it is where Cromwell grew to love wrestling. His high school coach, Ben Call, recalled recognizing Cromwell's potential early after he decided not to play basketball in high school.
"Big kid, very athletic — got him out into some open mats, and then the rest is basically history after that," Call said.
Cromwell discovered beach wrestling through a teammate at Doane College in Nebraska last year and it was a breath of fresh air.
“All my life wrestling, I've always thought about the success,” he said. “I've always been fixated on winning and the outcome. When it came to this, it was just fun. I loved it. I did it because it made me happy, and I think that's the switch that flipped in my head and why I became so successful in it. It actually made me happy, so I just picked it up and ran with it.”
Cromwell said the experience in Greece — which he noted was the birthplace of wrestling, the world’s oldest sport — went beyond the competition itself.
"Even apart from the wrestling, it was definitely a breathtaking experience,” he said. “Something you know I'll never forget.”
Call said watching Cromwell grow from a freshman to a world championships competitor has been deeply rewarding.
"There were definitely moments that we've shared with him being a high school kid and getting into a little bit of things here and there, but he trusted me. ... I never gave up on him, and he never gave up on me being a coach to him and leading him the right direction, the right path. Just seeing the growth, from where he came in as a freshman and now being able to travel over to Greece, gave me so much joy. That's basically a boy becoming a man.”
It sets an incredible example for other Mules wrestlers, which he now helps coach, and kids in the Lone Jack community.
"The opportunities that are out there for these kids that are from Lone Jack and are so in this fishbowl, they don't get to see the outside world and understand, ‘Hey, there are tons of opportunities out there. You just have to be willing to go take them,’” said Call, who has coached the Mules boys wrestling team for a decade and will transition exclusively to coaching the girls team this winter.
Cromwell isn’t finished either. In fact, he’s just getting started.
“I actually got some recent news from my (USA Wrestling) coaches that they're going to be taking me on the World Series in 2027,” Cromwell said. “I'm going to spend the entire year traveling the world. I'm going to go to every single stop in the World Series. There will be five stops, as well as the Pan American Championships in Peru.”
Between meets, Cromwell has been invited to train with other USA Wrestling athletes, several Kansas and Missouri area colleges and even with teams in Europe.
Cromwell said beach wrestling is a fast-paced version of the sport, complicated by fighting for traction inside the sandy circle used for matches.
Opponents score a point anytime they get an opponent to touch anything other than a hand or foot to the ground. The first to three points wins.
"The match can end in 5 seconds with a three-point throw, feet to back, right," Cromwell said. "You get taken down; they get a point. You get pushed out; they get a point. You get thrown to your back; match is over."

The end could be nigh for the iconic OP-1 according to a Highsnobiety interview.
Teenage Engineering founder and CEO Jesper Kouthoofd told Highsnobiety that it plans to stop making synths. And yes, that includes the iconic OP-1, which put the company on the map. TE isn’t just a music gear maker; it’s also a sought-after design firm. It’s collaborated with Ikea , Nothing , and Playdate , among others . But almost everything the company makes itself — the OP-1 , the OP-XY , EP-133 , TP-7 , et cetera — is music or audio-focused. Which makes the supposed decision to abandon the market all the more confusing.
Here’s the relevant quote from Highsnobiety :
Kouthoofd tells me that, as part of a reorganization last fall, he announced to his team he is planning to stop making synthesizers altogether. The OP-1 is no exception. Launched in 2011, it put Teenage Engineering on the map and has been central to its success ever since.
“Everyone was like, ‘What are you talking about?’ But I’ve come to the conclusion that, for us, the products aren’t the business,” Kouthoofd says. “We can be so much more than that.”
Teenage Engineering did not immediately return a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Hispanic Heritage Month: Israel Balderas helps students find their passion in a world ‘out of control’
articles.title_zh: Hispanic Heritage Month: Israel Balderas helps students find their passion in a world ‘out of control’
articles.content_orig:
A self-described “Texan American with a Mexican heart,” Assistant Professor of Journalism Israel Balderas says at the center of his sense of belonging at Elon are his students.
Israel Balderas is no stranger to the public eye. The First Amendment attorney and former television journalist regularly speaks with media outlets about current events, an extension of the work he does as an assistant professor of journalism at Elon University.
“As an academic, my relationship is going out in the name of Elon, even though I speak for myself,” said Balderas. “I’m always saying, ‘Here at Elon, we don’t make small plans. We’re always thinking bigger, and because we are a national school, what would help us to continue to be a national school?’ To me, my responsibility as an academic is to get my name out there.”
For Balderas, that work is closely connected to the sense of belonging he has found at Elon and the university’s teacher-scholar-mentor model. At the center of it all are his students.
“When my students leave, and the class is over, I say, ‘Love you. Mean it.’ And we throw the word love around a lot,” Balderas said. “But, to me, as a teacher, I think love from a teacher to a student is this idea, and it’s my ‘why.’ My ‘why’ is that I’m passionate about teaching students how to find their passion in a world that is out of control.”
Balderas began his journalism career as a freelance reporter and producer for several outlets in Washington, D.C. His coverage of the 2000 presidential election helped spur an interest in legal studies, as did a friendly competition with his sister over who could earn the higher score on the LSAT.
Growing up in a single-parent Hispanic household, Balderas said education was “non-negotiable.” He went on to earn his Juris Doctor from the Catholic University of America while working as a producer at FOX News Channel.
In the years that followed, Balderas worked for television stations across Florida, North Carolina and Texas. His work earned multiple industry accolades, including an Emmy for Best Continuing Coverage and recognition from the Radio Television Digital News Association of the Carolinas as best TV news anchor.
My ‘why’ is that I’m passionate about teaching students how to find their passion in a world that is out of control.
-Israel Balderas, assistant professor of journalism
Alongside his journalism career, Balderas took on legal work for the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law, We The Action and the Society of Professional Journalists. His pro bono work included representing migrant children at the U.S.-Mexico border and helping nonprofits navigate financial aid during the COVID-19 pandemic.
In 2017, Balderas left television news to spend more time with his family and transitioned to higher education, first teaching at a university in West Palm Beach, Florida, before joining Elon’s faculty in 2021.
“I love the mission of Elon University,” Balderas said. “The mission of Elon is that it ‘embraces its founder’s vision of an academic community that transforms mind, body, and spirit and encourages freedom of thought and liberty of conscience.’ And I said during my interview, that’s what a First Amendment professor teaches. That’s it.”
Journalism major Lily Molina ’27 took Balderas’ Media Law & Ethics course and says having a Latino professor in the journalism department made her feel welcomed as an aspiring Latina journalist.
“ I am really passionate about covering stories centered around my community, and Balderas has supported me in doing that. It’s comforting to have someone who I can speak Spanish to and not feel judged,” she said. “This is just one of the reasons why having diversity within departments is so important.”
A self-described “Texan American with a Mexican heart,” Balderas views Hispanic Heritage Month through the lens of the cultures that have shaped the United States.
“It’s about celebrating many cultures who have been able to adapt their cultures to this idea of ‘American citizen,’” he said. “What I love about Hispanic Heritage Month is that we get to show off the beauty of our diversity in a society that is diverse.”
Balderas describes that blending of cultures as a “stew,” one he sees reflected regularly on Elon’s campus. He points to El Centro, a space within the Center for Race, Ethnicity and Diversity Education that celebrates Latine and Hispanic cultures while sharing them with the broader Elon community.
“Every time I go to El Centro, there are kids from all over, and they’re all happy, and they’re ready to tell us about their abuelita (grandmother), they’re ready to tell us about their family,” Balderas said. “They’re ready to tell us about the history of their country. And in sharing all that, we get to build community together.”
As part of Hispanic Heritage Month, Elon University is sharing stories that celebrate the contributions, identities and experiences of students, faculty and staff. This month recognizes the rich histories and cultures of Hispanic and Latine communities, while also honoring the ways these traditions connect with and inspire people of all backgrounds. This month provides a special opportunity to honor Hispanic and Latine heritage, but it also serves as an invitation for all members of the university to engage, learn and celebrate together.

articles.title_orig: In Vienna and Beijing, the First Nuclear Clocks Begin to Tick
articles.title_zh: In Vienna and Beijing, the First Nuclear Clocks Begin to Tick
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain

            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles

Atomic clocks have made time and frequency the most precisely measured quantities in physics, progressing from microwave standards that realize the SI second 1 to optical clocks with unprecedented precision 2 . A nuclear clock transfers the frequency reference from an electronic to a nuclear transition and the uniquely low-lying, laser-accessible, isomeric transition in 229 Th currently offers the most practical route to compact, robust timekeeping and sensitive tests of fundamental physics 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 . Realizing such a clock requires turning spectroscopy of the 229 Th nuclear resonance 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 into a stable discriminator for steering a traceable oscillator. Here we demonstrate a 229 Th nuclear clock by stabilizing a continuous-wave, narrow-linewidth 148.4 nm vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) laser 18 to a resolved, weakly temperature-sensitive nuclear transition 17 , 19 in 229 Th:CaF 2 crystals 20 , 21 , 22 . A 10-μW VUV source generated by four-wave mixing in cadmium vapour 18 , 23 , 24 and phototube-based frequency modulation absorption readout provide a fast, high-signal-to-noise nuclear discriminator. The clock reaches a fractional frequency instability of \(5\times 1{0}^{-13}/\sqrt{\tau /{\rm{s}}}\) for averaging time τ . Clock-transition frequencies measured in two independently fabricated crystals agree at the 10 −13 level and are consistent with previous VUV-comb measurements on other 229 Th:CaF 2 crystals 17 . These results establish laser-addressed nuclei as operational clock references and provide a reproducible solid-state platform for compact nuclear clocks, nuclear quantum sensors and precision tests of fundamental physics.
Laser generation and laser spectroscopy are rooted in the electronic structure of atoms, molecules and solids. Nuclear transitions, by contrast, usually occur at energies far above typical electronic transitions, leaving most nuclear resonances beyond direct coherent access with conventional optical spectroscopy. The 229 Th isomer is a singular exception. Its transition energy lies in the vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) range, making it the only known nuclear transition that can be addressed directly with current laser technology. This coincidence opens a route to quantum coherent control of a nucleus and, in particular, to a nuclear clock, in which the frequency reference is shifted from the electronic shell to the atomic nucleus.
Decades of work established the existence and energy of this low-lying state 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 . The observation of radiative decay from 229 Th-doped crystals further showed that the isomer can remain long-lived in VUV-transparent hosts 13 , 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 . Building on these developments, direct laser excitation of the 229 Th isomer has been achieved recently 14 , 15 , 16 , 36 , and VUV-frequency-comb spectroscopy has enabled precision measurement of the nuclear transition frequency against optical atomic clocks 16 . In crystalline hosts, spectroscopy has further resolved the solid-state structure of the nuclear resonance, including quadrupole-split transitions 16 , site-dependent shifts 36 , 37 , temperature sensitivities 19 and reproducible transition frequencies across crystals 17 . Together with the macroscopic number of nuclei provided by a solid-state host 38 , 39 , 40 , these advances open the possibility of compact and field-deployable nuclear frequency references.
Another enabling element for clock operation is a continuous-wave VUV source at the nuclear resonance. Resonantly enhanced four-wave mixing in metal vapour 18 , 23 , 24 and randomly quasi-phase-matched SrB 4 O 7 (refs. 41 , 42 ) have provided routes to continuous-wave 148.4-nm radiation. Converting nuclear laser spectroscopy into clock operation requires combining, in a single system, a traceable narrow-linewidth VUV probe, a 229 Th-containing reference and a high-bandwidth, high-signal-to-noise readout of weak nuclear response, together with a demonstration of nuclear-transition-frequency reproducibility in independently prepared references.
In this work, we develop and integrate all the ingredients required for 229 Th clock operation. We upgrade the cadmium vapour four-wave-mixing source 18 to generate 10 μW of continuous-wave 148.4-nm radiation with an estimated sub-Hertz linewidth. We also fabricate, in a single growth run, a compact, high-quality 229 Th:CaF 2 crystal from a solution containing only 1.4 μg (10 kBq) of 229 Th. In fluorescence and absorption spectroscopy, we resolve a broad quadrupole-unresolved (QU) and a quadrupole-resolved (QR) structure comprising five narrow transitions, including line b, which is used for clock operation. Combining this traceable high-power VUV probe with home-grown crystals, we demonstrate the operation of the first 229 Th nuclear clock by using phototube-based frequency modulation absorption spectroscopy to generate the nuclear discriminator and close a feedback loop to line b. We then use the feedback-stabilized system to characterize the clock instability and test the reproducibility of the clock-transition frequency across two independently fabricated crystals and by comparison with previous VUV-comb measurements on other 229 Th:CaF 2 crystals 17 , 43 .
A near-simultaneous independent report has also demonstrated 229 Th nuclear clock operation using the randomly quasi-phase-matched SrB 4 O 7 VUV source, a highly doped 229 Th:CaF 2 crystal and photomultiplier-tube-based absorption readout 44 , building on related continuous-wave nuclear absorption spectroscopy with sub-nanowatt 148.4-nm light 45 .
We generate continuous-wave 148.4-nm radiation by resonance-enhanced four-wave mixing in cadmium vapour 18 , 23 , 24 . articles.title_orig: France suspends use of stun grenades to police student protests
articles.title_zh: France suspends use of stun grenades to police student protests
articles.content_orig:
France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials.
The disruption continued on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has defended the police response, after several groups complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.
In an address to the nation on Wednesday evening, he denied security forces had "orders to confront" the young people.
He said the government would look into the demands made by students and promised they would present a set of proposals at the end of October, ranging from renovating buildings to make more teachers available. He gave no further details.
The "anger of young people does not come from nowhere," he said.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "set alight or vandalised" to such an extent that they would be shut for several weeks, affecting 30,000 pupils.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt.
Nuñez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions.
"There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said as he confirmed the suspension of stun grenades - weapons which are considered non-lethal and send out small rubber pellets when they detonate.
The 15-year-old boy's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near the Auguste Béhal high school in the northern city near Lille.
Authorities have said he picked up the grenade which then exploded, but students have alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired. According to the local prefect, police had been confronted by more than 200 students throwing stones and fireworks.
The national secretary of policing union UNSA said he was sceptical about the move, saying it had been based "on emotion".
"We are dealing with increasingly violent people," Jean-Paul Nascimento told FranceInfo, cautioning that without the weapon to disperse crowds there may be more clashes at close quarters. "That's where there will perhaps be even more injuries," he warned.
Concerns have also been stoked by the case of a 14-year-old hit in the face with a tear gas grenade last week. The boy's lawyer said he had lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw in the incident at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, and a police officer has been charged.
And in a separate development on Wednesday, a 16-year-old suffered a serious hand injury outside a school in Strasbourg, reportedly while handling a mortar firework.
Prosecutors also said an investigation for attempted murder had been opened after a 17-year-old student protester complained an officer "held his head underwater" while trying to arrest him near a river in the north-eastern city of Belfort. French reports say the boy has himself been charged with aggravated assault for allegedly attacking the officer.
Addressing France's National Assembly on Wednesday, both Nuñez and Education Minister Geffray said the speed at which the protests had turned violent was unprecedented.
Geffray said dozens of headteachers and deputies had been injured, many deliberately so, and alleged the movement had been "very quickly infiltrated by ultra-violent groups".
"We have never seen anything like this," he said of the disorder which officials report has harmed more than 200 students and 700 police officers, and prompted more than 6,600 arrests.
Nuñez later said he found it "excessive to speak of police repression of the movement", insisting that officers were only acting in response to violence and damage.
The national coordinator of the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party said that it had taken "several children being maimed for life for Nuñez to give up using grenades against high school students".
The prime minister has accused LFI of trying to "sow chaos" during the protests ahead of elections to select President Emmanuel Macron's successor in April.
Its leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently second in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally - who on Wednesday said Macron was "always on the side of attacking the police".
The president held an emergency meeting late on Tuesday with Prime Minister Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis after almost a quarter of all lycées were disrupted by the day's protests - with government figures putting the number of protesters at more than 250,000.
Lecornu announced that schools should set aside half the day for students to voice their concerns, and noted on social media that an online consultation seeking their opinions had drawn 30,000 responses within a day.
But students' unions - who put the number of protesters at 450,000 - maintain a fourth round of demonstrations is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities, and told reporters they had requested a meeting with Lecornu due to a lack of "concrete measures" outlined so far.
The union representing school leaders told FranceInfo that a solution would require "something more than simple consultation periods", while the head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, told French radio on Wednesday: "We are telling M. Nuñez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint."

articles.title_orig: Trump’s SCOTUS succession dilemma: His favorite justices are also the court’s oldest
articles.title_zh: Trump’s SCOTUS succession dilemma: His favorite justices are also the court’s oldest
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is putting President Donald Trump on notice: If Democrats win control, they don’t intend to put “MAGA” judges on the courts.
“The bottom line is: One of the reasons we want to do everything we can to take back the Senate is not let Trump put such horrible justices — MAGA justices — on the Supreme Court and the lower courts,” Schumer said in response to a question from NBC News about a potential high court vacancy if Democrats win in 2026.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a senior member of the Judiciary Committee, said he doesn’t think a Democratic-led Senate would confirm a Trump pick for the Supreme Court either.
“Well, given the history of Trump nominees, I think it is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration,” Blumenthal said in an interview. “Because we’ve seen this movie, we know how it ends, which is a politician in robes who is following Trump’s orders on most major questions.”
The remarks highlight the high stakes of the 2026 election for Trump’s final two years when it comes to judicial nominees, especially for the Supreme Court if there’s a vacancy. None of the nine justices has signaled plans to retire, but speculation has centered on how long the two oldest justices — conservatives Clarence Thomas, 78, and Samuel Alito, 76 — will stay on the court. Justice Sonia Sotomayor and Chief Justice John Roberts are the next oldest justices, at 72 and 71, respectively.
Alito told CBS News in a recent interview that he considered retirement earlier this year, but ultimately decided against it.
“It’s something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term,” Alito said, while adding: “It’s too hard to predict what the political situation will be, and what any president might do with respect to a replacement.”
If Democrats win control of the Senate, they would have the power to determine which of Trump’s nominees for federal judicial postings get hearings and votes, including for a hypothetical Supreme Court vacancy.
But if Republicans keep control, the president will maintain his glide path to fill vacancies with his preferred nominees — adding to his nearly six-year total of 290 federal judges, including three Supreme Court justices during his first term. All of those judges have been confirmed under GOP Senate control.
Some Democrats say there should be no question of confirming a Trump pick after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., held a seat open for 10 months under President Barack Obama to let a Republican president fill it instead. (Justice Neil Gorsuch ultimately filled that vacancy.)
“No, we’ve got to do exactly what McConnell did to us,” Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said.
Gallego said he doesn’t want it to become a rule that no president can get a nominee confirmed by a Senate run by the opposing party. But at minimum, he wants Democrats to “even the scales.”
Beyond that, “I don’t think you know you want to go down that road,” the first-term Arizona Democrat said. “But clearly you know McConnell and Trump used, I would say, their power, whatever you want to call it, to change the makeup of the courts. And I think we have to start moving it back.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., who sits on the Judiciary Committee, said he wouldn’t count on Trump getting any Supreme Court nominee through a Democratic-led Senate.
“I don’t think it would be impossible. You know, there’s a slim possibility, very slim possibility,” Kennedy said. “But there’s a possibility that somebody would confuse me with Brad Pitt. I mean, it’s possible, but it’s not likely.”
Kennedy, like most U.S. senators quoted in this article, spoke before Alito’s comments to CBS News were published.
Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who took her late brother Lindsey Graham’s seat on the Judiciary Committee when she was appointed to the Senate, reacted directly to Alito’s remarks and connected it to her 2026 campaign for a six-year term.
“Should Justice Alito choose to retire next year, a Republican-majority Senate will be needed to vote and hopefully confirm a Supreme Court nominee from President Trump,” Graham wrote on X . “If Democrats control the Senate, they will not even allow a vote. And if they allow a vote, they will defeat a Trump-nominated candidate regardless of their qualifications.”
Another open question is how a Democratic majority would approach Trump judicial nominees for the lower courts.
Blumenthal said that one of his litmus tests for Trump judicial nominees up and down the courts is that they must be able to correctly answer who won the 2020 election, a question that various Trump nominees have refused to engage on as the president persists with false claims that it was stolen from him.
“We’ll stop a lot of these totally unqualified, ideologically right-wing nominees who won’t answer the question of who won the 2020 election,” Blumenthal said. “Among other questions.”
Some Democrats with a long memory haven’t forgotten that McConnell slowed nearly all judicial nominations to a crawl in Obama’s last two years, when the Kentucky Republican first took charge as Senate majority leader. McConnell saw it as payback for Democrats abolishing the 60-vote threshold for lower court judges in 2013, which at the time was part of a rapidly escalating judicial war between the parties.
Still, not all Democrats are willing to speculate on how they would deal with Trump’s judicial nominees.
Sen. Mazie Hirono, D-Hawaii, another member of the Judiciary Committee, paused and chuckled when asked if Democrats would confirm a Trump-nominated justice to the Supreme Court.
“Well, I don’t know. I can’t speak for my colleagues,” she said. “Let us just say that I would be very much for Supreme Court reform. ... One that allows every president to nominate two Supreme Court justices, and then they move on” to senior status .
Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., the current ranking member of the Judiciary Committee, is retiring after this Congress. Next in line to chair the panel, should Democrats capture the Senate, would be Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.
Whitehouse declined to engage when asked what the dynamic of judicial nominations would be if he becomes chairman.
Josh Orton, the president of the progressive judicial group Demand Justice, said his organization is “prepared to oppose any Trump nominee, regardless of when the vacancy happens.”
“On moral and political grounds, I don’t see any reason for Democrats to consider a Trump Supreme Court nomination,” Orton said, adding that Trump wants judges to be personally loyal to him, and would select them on that basis. “Any casual observer knows that Trump sees the Supreme Court generally as a political extension of himself — or that it should be.”
Just last month, Trump issued a lengthy criticism of the Supreme Court on Truth Social for ruling against him on mail-in ballots, tariffs and birthright citizenship. “The Supreme Court has really let our Country down. ... These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” he wrote. “They are merely a shell of their original selves.”
CORRECTION (Oct. 5, 2026, 12:55 p.m. ET): Due to an editing error, a previous version of this article misstated who ultimately filled the Supreme Court vacancy that arose at the end of President Barack Obama’s term. It was Justice Neil Gorsuch, not Brett Kavanaugh.
Sahil Kapur is a senior national political reporter for NBC News.
