articles.title_zh: Trump’s Texas two-step: From the Politics Desk
articles.content_orig:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk , a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
In today’s edition, we dig into yet another visit to Texas from the president. Plus, Andrea Mitchell examines what has — and hasn’t — happened since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
President Donald Trump is making his second trip in the past week to Texas tonight, highlighting how the midterm fight has shifted traditionally red terrain in the final stretch.
He’s set to rally in San Antonio for state Attorney General Ken Paxton and congressional candidate Carlos De La Cruz . Paxton remains locked in a tight and expensive battle with Democrat James Talarico . And De La Cruz’s race in the 35th District, which was redrawn in the redistricting process last year to be more favorable to Republicans, has been more competitive than expected. While Trump would have carried the district under its new lines by 10 points in 2024, the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the race as “lean Republican.”
Notably absent from tonight’s rally? Gov. Greg Abbott , who cited a scheduling conflict.“Well, first, whenever he does show up, it leads to excitement among the base, and he does a good job of getting the base organized and turning out,” Abbott said yesterday of Trump.
“Because of the schedule that I run, where I go to multiple cities a day doing events like this, already have events like this scheduled that day, and I will not be able to make it,” he added.
Abbott is also facing a tougher re-election battle than Republicans anticipated at the outset of the cycle: He won his last three races for governor by double digits.
But the broader political environment has proven treacherous for Republican candidates across the board. And now, national Democrats are under growing pressure to spend more resources on behalf of gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa , who is at a major financial disadvantage against Abbott.
Natasha Korecki reports that Latino leaders in Texas, including members of Congress, met with the Democratic Governors Association this morning to discuss Hinojosa’s campaign. In a letter, a group of Latino stakeholders in the state called on the DGA to “make a real meaningful investment of $3 million” into the race before early voting begins in less than two weeks.
The DGA recently committed $1 million to the race, while Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker announced he would send $1 million to her campaign after already giving $200,000. ( The New York Times first reported on those contributions.)
Meanwhile, Abbott isn’t the only Republican on the ballot this fall who appears to be seeking some distance from Trump. Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers said in a new ad today that “we need to end this tariff war now.” The party’s candidate for governor in the state, John James , also put daylight between himself and Trump on tariffs and the Iran war at a debate last night .
🥊 More from the debate stage: In the Maine Senate race , Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson traded attacks over Trump, the cost of living and abortion. In Georgia’s race for governor , Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson also sparred over Trump and the economy. And in the Iowa gubernatorial contest , Republican Zach Lahn ’s residency history was a major topic.
At dawn on a holiday weekend three years ago today, Israel was stunned when hordes of Hamas terrorists stormed across its border, slashing and and kidnapping revelers at an all-night music festival and rampaging through nearby settlements, or kibbutzim. In total, 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals, including 46 U.S. citizens, were killed, while 251 were taken hostage.
Thus began a war that shattered Israel’s confidence in its military superiority and ultimately transformed the region, sowing the seeds for the current war against Iran. Despite a ceasefire and hostage release, the conflict in the Gaza Strip and now the occupied West Bank continues at a slow burn with periodic outbreaks to this day.
How could Israel have been so taken by surprise? Although Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has blocked an official investigation into how his country’s vaunted military could have been so blindsided, NBC News has confirmed authoritative reports on the colossal intelligence failure, including a stunning account that an all-woman border patrol’s early warnings were dismissed by male superiors. Inexplicably, it took more than six hours after the massacre for the country to mobilize a response.
The human cost is incalculable. By the numbers, the Hamas-led Gaza Health Ministry estimates that about 75,000 people, including more than 44,000 children, have died in Gaza. Thousands more have been injured. Israel says it has lost 970 soldiers. Gaza has largely been leveled, its housing, schools and hospitals destroyed. The International Criminal Court, a United Nations entity that is not recognized by either Israel or the Trump administration, has cited both sides over allegations of war crimes. And the conflict has fueled cries of genocide against Israel by protesters in Europe and the U.S., an accusation that’s offensive to those in a country born as a refuge for survivors of the Holocaust.
Based on a Biden administration plan, Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner finalized a ceasefire and release of surviving hostages, as well as the return of hostage remains. The White House promises that its Board of Peace — a group of world leaders each pledging $1 billion to a nongovernment entity led by President Donald Trump — is supposed to be recruiting a multinational peace-keeping force to disarm Hamas and get Israel to withdraw to a border buffer zone. Trump has said the Gaza Strip could be rebuilt as “The Riviera of the Middle East.” None of that has taken place.
Now, Netanyahu faces a closely fought election in three weeks that has become a referendum on his conduct of the war in Gaza and failure to prevent it. His national security ministers are spearheading a campaign to seize as many Palestinian villages in the disputed West Bank as possible now as a hedge against a victory by a government less opposed to a Palestinian state. And Israel’s conduct of the war has become a political issue in the U.S. that could affect some of this year’s key midterm races as well as the Democratic Party’s nominating contest in 2028.
Fiona Glisson contributed research.
That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner.
If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com
And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here .

articles.title_orig: DNC sues to block Trump administration from using government funds for political ads
articles.title_zh: DNC sues to block Trump administration from using government funds for political ads
articles.content_orig:
Ads promoting the president have cost more than $12m and his Super Pac has refused to reimburse taxpayers
Sign up to The Stakes 2026: your weekly guide to the US midterms
The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration in federal court on Wednesday, asking a judge in Washington DC to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself, arguing that the ads are illegal government-sponsored propaganda .
The ads promoting Donald Trump , including one recycled from his 2024 presidential campaign, have cost taxpayers more than $12m so far, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.
Ken Martin, the DNC chair, said in a statement that Trump was misusing taxpayer dollars in “a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November. Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes.”
After a bipartisan backlash to the use of public money to promote himself during the final month of the midterm campaign season, Trump claimed on Monday that he would direct the Maga Inc Super Pac he controls to pay for the ads instead.
The next day, however, the White House said Trump’s political action committee would not reimburse taxpayers for the money it had already spent on the ads. Then, when the government unveiled a fifth ad in the series, celebrating Trump’s military intervention in Venezuela, it was also paid for by the US government.
The DNC complaint , filed in the US district court for the District of Columbia, alleges the ads violate federal law, including a ban on congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda”.
“President Trump personally directed this illegal activity. The White House office crafted the partisan campaign. The office of management and budget shifted $20m to pay for it. And US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has carried it out. These unlawful actions are ultra vires and violate the Administrative Procedure Act (APA),” the complaint states.
The suit also notes the first ad in the series features an image of Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, awarding Trump the so-called “Fifa peace prize” to support its case that the ads all violate a prohibition on the use of taxpayer funds for “self-aggrandizement”.
The complaint also references new polling from Reuters/Ipsos released on Tuesday which found that an overwhelming majority of Americans, 86%, ​called it inappropriate to use taxpayer funds for TV ads featuring the president around an election. The survey reported that about 80% of Republicans called the ads inappropriate, with only 17% of the president’s party approving of them.
after newsletter promotion
According to the suit, the ads have been broadcast on ABC, NBC, MS Now, CBS, CNN, Fox News and Newsmax, and appeared during popular NFL and college football games, and news and entertainment shows in which the president has been criticized, including Meet the Press, Jimmy Kimmel Live! and Saturday Night Live.
The federal lawsuit also includes details of another eight ads that have already been prepared for broadcast and were found “in a Dropbox account controlled by LMD Agency Inc, the government contractor bringing the ads to air”.
The ads ready to be broadcast include: one that celebrates the UFC fights staged at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June; one titled “God Made Trump”, a fan-created hymn of praise to Trump that was shown during the Republican midterm convention; one titled “Resilience”, which includes images of Trump announcing his candidacy for the presidency in 2015, then being charged in Fulton county, Georgia, in 2023 for conspiring to overturn the results of the 2020 election, and video of the assassination attempt on him during the 2024 election campaign; one titled “King of the Jungle”, which shows a lion hunting in the wild and disparages Trump’s political enemies, including former president Barack Obama. In February, Trump shared a racist video on social media that portrayed him as a lion and Barack and Michelle Obama as apes.
According to CNN , which gained access to the Dropbox last week, another ad in the series features attacks on Joe Biden, including the mocking image of the former president as an autopen installed by Trump on an exterior wall of the White House.

articles.title_zh: World of Warcraft: Forever- The Future of Skyborne Visual Updates
articles.content_orig:
The World of Warcraft development team began our journey into World of Warcraft: Forever with ambitions that grew and evolved over time. Our aim has always been to uphold the original WoW era aesthetic, while giving players more choice in how they experience Azeroth.
Over the course of development, we have been aligning on the right range of fidelity and what feels like it belongs in the WoW: Forever world and what does not. The team has learned much in the process, and that will continue to strengthen more with future content.
Along the way, there were some ideas the team wanted to explore that ultimately didn’t quite meet the consistency and cohesion we are aiming for. To align with our goals better, we are taking aim at updating some of those visuals for the future. Here is one example of how we are revisiting the High Definition (HD) Skyborne Druid forms.
We removed a bit of the softness, added more detailed fur textures, and adjusted the color saturation. The Skyborne are from an exotic environment, and their Druid forms reflect that, but we don't want that to be dissonant with the visual language of other creatures in the world.
In choosing to offer an SD or HD toggle for player characters, we focused on the pre-existing races from original World of Warcraft since many people have an attachment to those models. However, we have heard feedback that the HD Skyborne can be jarring by contrast when placed in the same world as the SD models and world, and we agree.
So, for those of us that prefer the look of SD models and want more choice, Skyborne player characters (and yes SD Druid forms) are in development and arriving early 2027. We look forward to sharing more information closer to that date. For now, here is an early work in progress image.
This is just the start of our journey, and the whole team is thrilled with the reception for World of Warcraft: Forever . As we continue refining this vision together, we look forward to what lies ahead—for the Horde! For the Alliance! Forever!

Austria, Poland and France shared the four Speed gold medals as the 2026 European youth season concluded in Germany
The 2026 World Climbing Europe Youth Series concluded in Leipzig, Germany, on 3 October, with Speed medals awarded in the Under 17 and Under 19 age categories.
Austria, Poland and France shared the four gold medals, while the host nation collected three medals in total: one silver and two bronze.
UNDER 17 GOLDS FOR HASELWANTER AND MYŚLIWIEC
Austria’s Lara Haselwanter won the women’s Under 17 title in 7.30 seconds in the gold-medal race, as Slovenia’s Zoja Leskovar fell and took silver. Germany’s Lea Voigt secured bronze on home soil, clocking 9.08 against Italy’s Carolina Mariani, who also slipped and did not complete her race.
The men’s Under 17 gold-medal race was an all-Polish contest, with Maksymilian Myśliwiec taking gold in 5.83 seconds after Antoni Marcisz fell. Germany’s Maximilian Ruhland completed the podium, winning the bronze-medal race in 8.48 ahead of compatriot Moritz Müller, who clocked 9.42.
FRANCE SECURES DOUBLE GOLD IN UNDER 19 EVENTS
Eva-Lina Rymasz claimed women’s Under 19 gold for France, winning in 7.88 seconds ahead of Italy’s Alice Marcelli, who finished in 8.47. Ukraine’s Mariia Shymkova took bronze in 8.44 after Germany’s Mina Josephine Schultz slipped and fell in the bronze-medal race.
France’s Léo Grosset added men’s Under 19 gold to his country’s medal tally. Grosset clocked 5.23 in the final against Germany’s Mika Scherer, who fell but took silver. Switzerland’s Gilles Meili won bronze in 4.93 against fellow Swiss climber Sofiane Vial, who was unable to complete the race.
Following the release of next year's international competition calendar, the 2027 European events calendar will also be presented in the coming days.
All European events have been live streamed on the World Climbing Europe YouTube channel and are available on demand. News and updates about all World Climbing events will be available on the World Climbing website , and on the Federation’s digital channels: Facebook , Instagram , LinkedIn , Threads , TikTok , X , YouTube , and exclusively for the Chinese audience, Douyin, Weibo , and Xiaohongshu.

In this file photo, smoke rises from a burned house in Gawdu Zara village, northern Rakhine state, Myanmar, Sept. 7, 2017, where the vast majority of the country’s 1.1 million Rohingya lived.
Malaysia recently returned 1,500 Rohingya refugees back to Myanmar, despite concerns for their safety. The persecuted Muslim minority is essentially “stateless” in its own country. Myanmar does not recognize them as citizens, even though many have lived there for generations, before being violently expelled.

articles.title_orig: Lululemon poaches Athleta CEO as new chief product officer
articles.title_zh: Lululemon poaches Athleta CEO as new chief product officer
articles.content_orig:
Lululemon announced Wednesday that Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger is joining the company as president and chief product officer, effective later this month.
The move marks the latest shake-up among the top executives in the increasingly competitive athleisure space: Gauger joined Athleta from Nike only last year.
Lululemon said Gauger's job is a newly created role. It also appointed Joseph Godsey as chief operating officer. Alongside the new announcements, Lululemon also said Nikki Neuburger, the company's chief brand and product activation officer, and Ted Dagnese, its chief supply chain officer, are leaving in November to "pursue other opportunities."
"We are establishing a deeply experienced leadership team that will work in a more coordinated manner, aligned around the strategy and execution that delivers the most impact for our guests, our communities, and our business," Lululemon CEO Heidi O'Neill said in a statement. "That starts with putting product, design, and innovation at the center of how we operate, with the focus and accountability to create a stronger pipeline of differentiated product to raise the bar for our guests across every touchpoint, in stores and online."
In a statement provided to CNBC, Athleta parent company Gap confirmed Gauger has left the company. It said Erika Everett, the brand's current chief marketing officer, will oversee the brand CEO role in the interim.
"We have been actively shaping Athleta's next chapter and the changes needed to position the brand for long-term growth," Gap said in its statement. "This transition enables us to accelerate that work, strengthen our connection with customers, and unlock Athleta's full potential."
Separately, Lululemon said it is also searching for a chief brand officer, a chief communications officer and a chief technology officer.
O'Neill took the helm of Lululemon last month after the athleisure company saw more than a year of disappointing sales performance in the midst of a proxy battle, drawing criticism from founder Chip Wilson.

articles.title_orig: Pacific News Minute: World Bank backs Tonga with $15M grant to create jobs
articles.title_zh: Pacific News Minute: World Bank backs Tonga with $15M grant to create jobs
articles.content_orig:
The World Bank is backing a series of measures to improve the economy of Tonga. The Pacific Island nation is facing a number of challenges, and the first goal is helping with job creation.
The World Bank says that more than one in four Tongans are unemployed.
Residents lack access to education or training, and that means that many go overseas to look for jobs.
By some estimates, nearly a third of the country's economic activity comes from remittances — money sent home by Tongans working overseas.
The World Bank is supporting a program to widen economic opportunity with a $15 million grant.
Tonga's First Growth and Jobs Development Policy Financing is the first of a two-part program.
The World Bank says the new operation backs government reforms to strengthen workforce skills, improve conditions for private investment and advance better management of Tonga's ocean resources.
The bank notes that a development policy grant does not create jobs overnight.
Its value depends on whether reforms are carried out clearly.
For households facing underemployment, the real test will be whether more Tongans can find proper training and paid work without leaving the country.

On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.

He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.”

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Claws Back Land in the Donbas, Thwarting a Russian Push
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Claws Back Land in the Donbas, Thwarting a Russian Push
articles.content_orig:
In January of this year, the "NC13" strike UGV unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade tested a new tactic deep behind Russian lines. Since then, the unit has successfully carried out more than 100 similar operations, turning what began as an experiment into a proven combat system.
The new tactic was named "Gryphon" in honor of a service member from the unit who went missing in action in 2023 while carrying out a combat mission near Andriivka in the Donetsk region. It was in this area, near Bakhmut, that Oscar-winning Ukrainian director Mstyslav Chernov filmed the documentary "2000 Meters to Andriivka" during a different Ukrainian counteroffensive.
The concept behind the new tactic involves deploying kamikaze UGVs, essentially ground robots, deep behind enemy lines using heavy bomber drones. After landing, the robotic systems continue moving toward their targets and can be used to strike key positions, logistics, and personnel while also creating disruption in the enemy rear.
The "NC13" unit was also behind an operation that drew significant international attention about a year ago, when Ukrainian forces captured Russian positions without deploying infantry, using only UGVs and drones.
As a result, two Russian service members surrendered to the robotic systems, after which the machines escorted them to Ukrainian positions as prisoners of war.
Today, the new tactic is part of the Third Army Corps' large-scale operation known as "Vivaldi." Since the start of the offensive, Ukrainian forces have liberated 176 square kilometers of territory (68 square miles ) .
According to the Office of the President of Ukraine, Russian forces suffered more than 5,000 casualties, including those killed, wounded, and captured, during the first three stages of the operation. It is currently known that Ukrainian forces have taken 250 Russian service members as prisoners of war (POWs). The Third Army Corps separately reported 2,000 Russian personnel casualties during the latest stage alone.
Approximately 80% of logistics and 90% of wounded evacuation for Ukrainian troops during all three stages of the operation were carried out by unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs.
"NC13" commander Mykola Zinkevych, call sign "Makar," explains how the new "Gryphon" tactic works, how the idea of air-dropping ground robots emerged, what happened during the first operations, how Russian forces are reacting to the technology, and why he believes Ukraine is shaping the future of technological warfare.
He also discusses how Western partners are becoming less able to understand Ukrainian military technologies and, more broadly, the needs of modern warfare.
Can you please explain, in general, what this new tactic involves?
In general, this is a sabotage-operation tactic that was fully planned, developed, and implemented by the "NC13" strike unmanned ground systems unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade.
The tactic is genuinely new and has no equivalent anywhere in the world because no one had previously deployed unmanned ground vehicles from unmanned aerial vehicles.
The concept itself is that, using heavy bombers, we drop small ground-based kamikaze systems deep into enemy territory, at a distance of 5 to 15 kilometers (3 to 9.3 miles ) . From there, we carry out different sabotage operations: eliminating enemy personnel, destroying logistics, and so on.
When did you begin using this tactic? Any first operation is essentially a test. How confident were you that it would work?
We carried out the first operation about eight months ago (in January 2026- UP).
We spent quite a long time developing the tactic itself and modifying the equipment because standard ground-based kamikaze systems are not designed for this kind of use.
The engineers spent a great deal of time making it work. The pilots also had to learn how to operate with these systems and deploy them correctly. The planning department, accordingly, spent a lot of time preparing the operation.
But when it worked for the first time, the excitement was incredible. Our first operation went 15 kilometers (9.3 miles ) deep behind enemy lines. We deployed two ground-based kamikaze systems near the target, and from there, the systems themselves moved into the shelter.
It was an enemy staging point where personnel were brought in. They would stop there to rest before moving on to carry out their missions. We eliminated that staging point using two ground-based kamikaze systems.
What was the enemy's reaction? What did it look like from their side?
In fact, the enemy did not understand what had happened, what system had been used, what had struck them, or what tactic we were employing.
Even now, it remains a major surprise for them because we operate in different sectors within the Third Army Corps' area of responsibility.
We combine different technologies in order to change the rules on the battlefield.
We have been able to strike the enemy from the air at significant depth for quite some time. We have also been using unmanned ground vehicles to strike enemy forces for a while.
But this combination (UGV + UAV) allows us to operate at greater depth, in areas where the enemy does not expect to be reached and where they feel relatively safe. So we are going to take that freedom away from them.
How many such operations have been carried out so far?
More than one hundred. We always work systematically. If something works once, twice, or three times, we still do not consider it a fully established capability because it could be accidental.
But when something is carried out more than ten times, it becomes a systematic approach. We have SOPs, standard operating procedures, in place for this tactic: how to use it, where it can be implemented, and what its capabilities are.
It can be used for reconnaissance, mining deep behind enemy lines, striking targets, hunting moving enemy personnel, disrupting logistics, and more. We have fully developed this tactic, identified all of its capabilities, and now use it as a full-fledged tool on the battlefield.
War in general, and especially Russia's war against Ukraine, is a war of speed. Everything depends on who can come up with something new and adapt faster. Are the Russians already trying to do something similar?
I am confident that we are far ahead of the enemy. Even when it comes to the systematic use of strike unmanned ground vehicles on the battlefield, which we have been doing for about a year, the enemy is still far behind.
So when it comes to tactics like "Gryphon," which we are discussing today, there is still a very large gap between us and them.
But I would not rule out the possibility that, over time, the enemy will begin copying this approach and using similar methods.
In fact, during more than 100 successful missions, there have been many almost meme-like moments when the enemy had no idea what they were looking at and would actually approach the robots to inspect them.
There was one occasion when we managed to completely disrupt a Russian mechanized assault that had been planned for foggy weather conditions. At the time, we were actively targeting one of the enemy's logistics routes. We eliminated several personnel over the course of the day.
They started to panic because they did not understand what was happening. They thought a sabotage and reconnaissance group, or SRG, had broken through into their rear. As a result, they canceled the mechanized assault they had planned for that day.
So these small robots can create very significant disruption.
In general, there was serious panic among enemy forces at the depth where we were operating. And panic is actually very important because if we create panic within enemy ranks, they begin to have problems controlling their personnel. Soldiers start refusing to carry out missions, which then creates panic at the command level because commanders do not understand what is happening in their rear, and so on.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: Nicolás Maduro and his wife expected to face new charges over alleged torture of Americans
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: Nicolás Maduro and his wife expected to face new charges over alleged torture of Americans
articles.content_orig:
Prosecutors in New York are expected to bring new charges against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan government custody in recent years, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation.
An announcement could come as soon as Thursday, the people said.
The new charges relate to what the US government has said was the wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens in Venezuelan prisons during the time Maduro led a repressive regime in Venezuela, the people briefed on the investigation said.
Investigators have also discussed charging several additional people for their alleged role in the torture of Americans, according to a source familiar with the matter.
CNN has reached out to lawyers for Maduro and Flores.
Maduro and his wife were captured in a US military raid in January from the presidential palace in Caracas. They have pleaded not guilty to narcoterrorism conspiracy and other charges and are held without bail in New York.
Flores is expected to appear at a hearing Thursday where her lawyer will ask that she be moved to house arrest ahead of trial.
Maduro’s lawyer is challenging the legality of the arrest and argues the former president should have immunity since the alleged conduct occurred while he was in office.
The Venezuelan government is not joining in claiming immunity on his behalf, according to the prosecution.
Nicolas Maduro heads back to court arguing that the US is trying to hamstring his defense
More than a dozen Americans were detained by the Maduro government, which was accused by US government and advocates of using them as political pawns.
Several of the Americans have spoken out about the torture say they were subjected to while they were imprisoned. Matthew Heath and Osman Khan, who were freed in a prisoner swap in October 2022, alleged in a lawsuit that they were subjected to waterboarding, electrocution, threats of sexual assault, use of mind-altering drugs, and periods of solitary confinement. Heath, a US Marine veteran, attempted suicide while he was detained.
The “CITGO 6,” a group of six American oil executives who were lured to Venezuela in 2017 and detained for nearly five years, also say they were subjected to brutal conditions while in Venezuelan detention. In lawsuits filed against their employer — Citgo — Tomeu Vadell, Alirio Jose Zambrano and Jose Luis Zambrano said they were subjected to torture while imprisoned.
All of them had been held in the notorious General Directorate of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM) — which was “responsible for arbitrary detentions, ill-treatment and torture of political opponents and their relatives,” according to a United Nations report.
That report found that DGCIM “routinely resorted” to torture practices “including electric shocks, suffocation with plastic bags, waterboarding, beatings, sexual violence, water and food deprivation, stress positions and exposure to extreme temperatures” in order to “extract information and confessions, intimidate, and punish the detainees.”

articles.title_orig: PA measles outbreak tops 1,000 cases, largest since disease was eliminated
articles.title_zh: PA measles outbreak tops 1,000 cases, largest since disease was eliminated
articles.content_orig:
Pennsylvania’s explosive measles outbreak is now the largest the US has seen since the highly infectious virus was declared eliminated in 2000. With well over 1,000 cases, it’s the largest on record since 1991.
Pennsylvania’s health officials reported 1,078 measles cases in all of 2026 as of this afternoon. That includes 12 cases in January and March, with the remaining 1,066 cases since April , when the current outbreak began. The tally includes 145 cases recorded in the last seven days and 74 identified since the previous update on Monday. Health officials noted that 40 of the 74 cases added today were from more than two weeks ago and are just now being recorded.
Among the cases, there have been 207 hospitalizations and five deaths— a newborn , a 6-week-old , an 18-year-old , a 20-year-old , and a 40-year-old . All of the deaths occurred during the current outbreak in people who were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated.
With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, measles outbreaks and cases have come roaring back in the past few years. A large outbreak in Texas that spanned January­–August 2025 ended with 762 cases , while an outbreak in South Carolina ended in April with 997 cases , the previous record holder. Pennsylvania exceeds that handily with its 1,066 outbreak-linked cases as of today. With 34 new infections reported since Monday, the outbreak does not appear to be close to ending.
Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. Elimination is earned and maintained with vaccination rates that prevent continuous transmission of the virus during a 12-month period. In November, experts at the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO)—which acts as a regional office for the World Health Organization—will review data on whether the US has lost its measles elimination status. Experts widely expect the US has lost the status. Canada lost its elimination status in 2025.
The last measles outbreak that was larger than the current one in Pennsylvania was an outbreak in New York, which spanned 1990–1991 and infected more than 4,500 in all.
Earlier this week, New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency over rising measles cases there. There have been at least 108 cases in the state. The emergency declaration expands the pool of healthcare workers who can provide measles vaccinations, newly including paramedics, advanced EMS providers, pharmacists, and midwives. It also allows nurses, in addition to physicians, to order measles tests.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” Hochul said in a statement. “That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting 3,887 measles cases nationwide for the year. That is the highest tally in the US since 1991, when there were 9,643 cases. Experts are becoming yet more anxious as measles outbreaks stretch into the fall; in the pre-vaccine era, measles was typically a virus of the late winter and early spring . Experts are concerned that spread could accelerate further in favorable conditions.

articles.title_orig: Israelis mourn Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians in Gaza languish in ruins of the war it sparked
articles.title_zh: Israelis mourn Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians in Gaza languish in ruins of the war it sparked
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani released a statement on the three-year anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks in Israel that has sparked outrage from Jewish leaders.
Mamdani faces renewed scrutiny over his views on the war. He has condemned the Oct. 7 attacks while also sharply criticizing Israel's response and describing it as a genocide.
His statement on Wednesday said the suffering did not begin nor end that day, and "it has continued through Israeli government's devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers. It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7. On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others. We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss. The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government's devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians—including more than 21,000 children. Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed. That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing. Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them - all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes. Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment. To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity."
It is Mamdani's first Oct. 7 anniversary as mayor, and his planned appearances throughout the day drew close attention from both supporters and critics, including an appearance at a vigil in Union Square Wednesday night, where the mayor was booed upon arrival.
The attack by Hamas killed nearly 1,200 people and resulted in 251 hostages being taken. Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza has resulted in thousands of Palestinian deaths.
Joe Potsanik of the New York Board of Rabbis says the mayor's statement was insensitive, at best.
"I wish I could say people were surprised, but they weren't," Potsanik said. "This is a day of mourning for us. Just give us that day. We can have all the other discussions, debates, on different days. But don't do it today."
The ADL released a statement in response to Mamdani's and accused him of "weaponizing a day meant for mourning."
"@NYCMayor, not once do you say 'Jews.' On Oct. 7, Hamas-led attackers murdered civilians, committed sexual violence, mutilated bodies and took hostages. You are weaponizing a day meant for mourning the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust to recycle your usual antizionist talking points. The city with the largest Jewish population outside Israel deserves a mayor who can honor the dead without exploiting them."
The Israeli Consulate, which had invited Mamdani to view Oct. 7 footage in the days leading up to the anniversary, issued a fiery statement that said in part:
"The mayor's statement is a disgrace, shame, and insult to the memory of those who were murdered on October 7. It is still not too late to attend our screening this evening of the October 7 footage and see with your own eyes, for the first time, the monsters you support," Amb. Ofir Akunis said.
Akunis said "anyone with a heart" should be ashamed of Mamdani's response.
"Mamdani, displaying a shocking lack of basic humanity, continues to spread antisemitic blood libels against the Jewish state. New York City should be appalled that its mayor shows such contempt for the memory of those who were murdered," Akunis concluded.
Mamdani campaigned as a fierce defender of Palestinian rights. As mayor, he's struggled to find a balance. He celebrates Jewish holidays and denounces the Israeli prime minister, yet he's alienated some of his core supporters while failing to reassure many Jewish New Yorkers that he will protect them from antisemitism.

As those gathered commemorated eight decades, alumni—some in person and some recorded online—voiced how their experience at the institute changed their lives.
WCC programme director for Unity, Mission, and Ecumenical Formation Rev. Dr Kuzipa Nalwamba, posed the question: “ What did Bossey give you that you could not have received elsewhere?”
From life-changing conversations to lifelong friends, alumni voices their gratitude for the institute, the faculty, and for each other.
The new Bossey Alumni Network is a digital space for alumni to reconnect. Free of charge, it will be a source of communication and news.

articles.title_orig: Rubio Urges Europe to Awaken From ‘Slumber’ and Uphold Western Dominance
articles.title_zh: Rubio Urges Europe to Awaken From ‘Slumber’ and Uphold Western Dominance
articles.content_orig:
In the golden light of an Athens evening, with the Acropolis over his shoulder, Marco Rubio hardly looked like a man planning to ride off into a political sunset.
The secretary of state’s speech in Greece on Wednesday will surely reignite speculation around his future presidential intentions. It implicitly positioned him as both the heir to and the modernizer of the “America First” movement — just weeks before the 2028 race roars into life after the midterm elections.
Rubio depicted the West as a continuous inheritance dating from Ancient Greece to modern America, epitomizing “individuality and relentless ambition, daring exploration and invention” as well as duty and heroism. But he warned that the civilization, ashamed of its achievements and embarrassed by its past, risked “atrophy, servitude and decline.”
“Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power,” Rubio said, giving himself some political cover for the high-profile appearance.
One interpretation is that this was yet another bid to retroactively impose doctrinal coherence on Trump’s erratic foreign policy of Iran war-style gut calls, power grabs and a transactional approach to resources.
And Rubio is just the latest administration official to bemoan Europe’s supposed decline; failure to tackle mass immigration; and prioritization of the “global community” over national interest. This canon was hallmarked by Vice President JD Vance’s stemwinder in Munich last year.
Yet he was seeking something deeper, at times, sketching the framework of a post-MAGA foreign policy in which US sovereignty and action remain paramount, while​ reinvigorating friendships shattered by Trump’s hostility.
“We must rebuild our institutions and alliances” to face new great power rivalries and respond to a “new universe” of threats and attacks, Rubio said.
His comments also reinforced a message to decayed European militaries that the US now expects alliances to offer tangible military multipliers to Washington. It was a hint that while nothing will be the same after Trump, a future Republican president might still value updated transatlantic ties.
Rubio also seemed to be fusing three strands of traditional GOP foreign policy — the muscular internationalism of Ronald Reagan, the realism of Richard Nixon and Trump’s coercive nationalism. He might also have been trying to make sense of his own political evolution from aspirational conservatism to his current, darker worldview. (Rubio’s critics portray his conversion to MAGAism as the cynical act of a political chameleon desperate for power.)
The speech was also jarring and contradictory.
He was the latest Trump acolyte to travel to Europe to explain Europe’s history to Europeans and to adopt an idealized view of Western civilization that fits the needs of America’s Christian nationalist right.
When Rubio laments eroded national sovereignty, like Vance, he seems oblivious to enduring national and cultural differences distinguishing French, German, Italian, and other European citizens. He ignored gruesome history that led late 20th-century leaders to constrain raging nationalism within shared political and economic structures.
And while Trump’s team believes something is rotten in Europe, many Europeans perceive a corrupt and increasingly authoritarian American is most to blame for obliterating Western values. Noting that “passions” have rocked the alliance, Rubio used a deceptive euphemism for Trump’s bullying.
Rubio’s lionizing of the ancient Greeks as foundational to the US also overlooked the founders’ concern that their direct democracy encouraged factionalism and promoted demagogues. Their answer was the Electoral College.
Some Europeans will be offended by Rubio’s speech. But he’s seen by allies as the most conventional and sympathetic Trump foreign policy official, so his comments may be less provocative than rebukes by Vance or Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Inevitably, such an ambitious speech using the optics of a major campaign address will stir presidential speculation. Visually, Rubio’s setting recalled then-Sen. Barack Obama’s hilltop speech at the Citadel in Amman, Jordan, in 2008.
A Rubio run in 2028 seems problematic with Vance in pole position as the vice president. But whether he next takes aim at the White House in two years, in 2032, or later, Rubio showed the world Wednesday his ambition is unquenched.

articles.title_orig: Supporting Workers in an AI World
articles.title_zh: Supporting Workers in an AI World
articles.content_orig:
Take a closer look at the "Make AI Work for Americans Act," and learn why it's important to help workers and families navigate AI disruption.
While there’s no consensus on exactly how artificial intelligence will affect workers, it’s clear that the technology will change who works and how they work. On September 24, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly introduced a bill called the Make AI Work for Americans Act . It prioritizes helping workers and families navigate the disruption that AI will cause through a federal trust fund paid for by the large AI companies set to profit most from AI’s boom.
In the past three years, the cumulative value of AI-linked firms has increased by $27 trillion across the value of the entire U.S. stock market; this accounts for 36% of value. There have been persistent concerns about whether this enormous spending—including on physical infrastructure and software development—is part of a bubble . Right now, this  technology is important to economic growth, as AI spending accounted for 40% of U.S. economic growth in the past year.
There are growing concerns about what the growth of AI means for American workers. OpenAI predicted that in the short term, 18% of jobs were at risk of automation, and 24% may see declining employment as the composition of tasks within occupations shifts.
Some estimates have found that of the highly AI-exposed workers, about 70% may be able to adapt fairly easily. But adaptation will likely be harder for over 6 million workers who are primarily employed in clerical and administrative roles.
What we can say now is that it’s likely that the effects of AI on workers will be concentrated in certain occupations. Last month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released AI exposure categories organized by occupation that track how well the capabilities of AI match job tasks, and over 200 occupations are facing very high exposure , such as customer service representatives and web developers. The billion (trillion?) dollar question is whether occupations that are highly exposed will be able to adapt .
It’s also clear that people are worried about how AI is going to impact their jobs. A 2026 poll on AI found that 7 in 10 Americans think that AI will cut jobs. Polling from Groundwork Collaborative and Ipsos found that only 6% of respondents believe that the benefits of AI will mostly or all go to workers, and two-third of workers say that AI will make work harder, not easier.
Workers are doing their best to keep up, and a March 2026 national survey found that to compete with AI tools or avoid potential layoffs, 81% of workers are changing their behavior at work.
In Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, universities are focused on developing technologies for physical AI , and the city is now home to 100 AI and robotics organizations. At the same time, Pittsburgh residents have pushed back against data centers due to their impact on the environment, pollution, and energy costs. Allegheny County is considering prohibiting data center development on county-owned land, and Pennsylvania has slowed data center development statewide.
In Iowa, rural communities like Salix are pushing back against data center projects; eight counties in the state already have moratoriums on data center development. Across the country, rural counties account for about two-thirds of planned data center projects, but they tend to see fewer benefits from these investments compared to cities. When a data center opens in a county, employment rises on average by about 3.5% and wages by 5%, but the gains from investment are experienced far more in urban counties than rural ones.
A third of South Carolinians believe that their employers will not protect them from having their jobs replaced by AI. At the same time, companies like Google are investing billions in the state’s cloud and AI infrastructure, i.e. data centers : Google’s 2025 investment is one of the largest technology investments in state history at $9 billion dollars .
Legislation like the Make AI Work for Americans Act is an important step and crucial part of supporting workers and their communities through this AI disruption. Importantly, it asks the companies profiting most from this technology to invest in the workers facing changing labor opportunities.
Heather Boushey is a professor of practice at the Kleinman Center. Boushey served in the Biden administration as a member of the Council of Economic Advisers and chief economist to the President’s Investing in America cabinet.

articles.title_orig: Three years after Oct.7, Chapel Hill native Keith Siegel and his wife reflect on survival and hope
articles.title_zh: Three years after Oct.7, Chapel Hill native Keith Siegel and his wife reflect on survival and hope
articles.content_orig:
Sadness, sorrow, and gratitude...a mixture of heavy emotions describes how Chapel Hill native Keith Siegel and his wife, Aviva, are feeling exactly three years after Hamas militants kidnapped them and dozens of others, killing 1,200 people.
"I always feel that when there's something really bad that you have to prepare yourself for it, you take your time," Aviva told WRAL News in an interview. "It doesn't happen only on the day. It happens like a couple of weeks before."
Aviva was released by Hamas more than a month after she was kidnapped. She said she has just recently begun to feel free.
"I've just started to feel free lately, and feel like you know things are a little bit different, and it's a trauma we're carrying it, and it's going to take time," she said.
Keith was released on February 1, 2025, after Israel and Hamas agreed to a five-week ceasefire. He survived 484 days of torture, along with a lack of information, sanitation, food, and water.
"I have been thinking a lot about how grateful I am to be alive and to be back reunited with my family, and that's amazing," he told WRAL News. "But together with that, I also feel so so sorry and sad for all of the people that didn't survive, and all of those that were injured physically, emotionally, and I think there's so so many of those, including ourselves, that are dealing with trauma, and I guess will be dealing with trauma forward."
Aviva described the torture they faced and the conditions they survived in during that time. She talked about how Hamas militants made Keith dig his own grave.
She documented what happened in detail and wrote a book called 'Survived to Tell' to share their truth.
"It's really a victory that Keith is here, and that I'm here, and that we could share the truth," Aviva said. "It's going to give everybody...the strength to understand that we, as grown-ups, have to speak and and just be sure that the next generations will have a better life, and that nothing like that will ever ever happen to the next generations."
As conflict persists in the Middle East, including in Israel, they are still clinging on to hope for peace.
"Just hoping and praying for peace all over the world in Israel and everywhere else, and so people will be able to live in peace and in security, and to have a good life," Keith said. "Life is short. Life is precious, and the leaders of ours and all over the world, it's their responsibility to prioritize stabilization and peace."
Pain and trauma still persist for Keith and Aviva. They appreciate all the support from the Triangle.
"Just coming to realize so many caring people, so many people that support us not even knowing us, and just working and advocating for our release and showing care and support in many many ways... It's very very moving, and it's very very uplifting, and it brings me a lot of optimism," Keith said. "Just thinking that things are good, things will be much better, and there are many many caring people that will be a part of that."

articles.title_orig: LACMA’s Alexander Calder Erewhon Smoothie Is What the Art World Deserves
articles.title_zh: LACMA’s Alexander Calder Erewhon Smoothie Is What the Art World Deserves
articles.content_orig:
Imagine you’re a hotshot young New York gallerist whose rapidly rising artist has been invited to show in a group exhibition at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA). But between this fall’s booths at Frieze London and Art Basel Paris, a detour to Venice, and micromanaging your unpaid interns, you can only go for a day. So, tragically, there’s no time to fit in your regular visit to Erewhon, for which there’s simply no New York equivalent, especially because the $36,000 initiation fee for the Kith Ivy padel club that houses the city’s only Erewhon tonic bar is prohibitive in this art market.
Well, I have good news for the few who can relate to these circumstances: LACMA announced this week that the Erewhon pop-up in its new David Geffen Galleries will now serve as the museum’s permanent cafe. Housed in a glass box beneath Peter Zumthor’s sprawling $720 million “ designed to disorient ” structure, the Erewhon cafe faces out toward Alexander Calder’s recently restored fountain, “ Three Quintains (Hello Girls) ” (1964).
Calder’s tripartite mobile is also the inspiration for a new (and pre-distressed) capsule apparel collection and a signature LACMA smoothie, made from organic mango, mandarin, pineapple, strawberry, and lion’s mane. The beverage's unnatural gray hue resembles the concrete of Zumthor’s design — only floating with blobs of Calderesque colors.
“This integration represents the perfect synergy between two brands inextricably rooted in Los Angeles culture,” Elizabeth Wiatt, senior vice president of strategic partnerships at LACMA, said in a press statement.
Much like the well-intentioned art world, whose ecosystem becomes more optimized but also more expensive and materialistic with each day, Erewhon is a far cry from the Taoist principles that guided its founders, Aveline and Michio Kushi, who established the first location in Boston in 1966. Today, the health-conscious “ premium ” grocery chain has become synonymous with a particular status-centric idea of LA, offering adaptogenic cocktails, celebrity-collaboration smoothies, and absurd oddities like a $12 cup of “ Sacred Water .”
For a museum that recently hosted the star-studded unveiling of Ed Ruscha's poster for Alejandro González Iñárritu’s new film Digger (2026), the Erewhon partnership is fitting. After all, it holds up a mirror to today's world, wherein overpaying for a smoothie somehow makes it more delectable, and institutional and commercial industry partnerships made under the guise of "community" are normalized.
Look no further than Erewhon President Josephine Antoci's euphemistic statement about the new LACMA cafe: “It’s a place for all to gather and make memories for years to come.”

articles.title_orig: Mike Flanagan Addresses Some of Those ‘Carrie’ Twists
articles.title_zh: Mike Flanagan Addresses Some of Those ‘Carrie’ Twists
articles.content_orig:
By Christopher Campbell | Published October 1, 2026
TAGGED AS: Horror , streaming , TV
Yet another adaptation of Stephen King’ s Carrie is arriving this month, and the first reviews of the full series mostly say the idea was worth repeating. Mike Flanagan , who has made a few movies and series based on King’s work, returns to television with his latest, a reimagining of the 1974 horror novel of the same name. In this incarnation, Summer H. Howell plays the title character, a bullied high schooler who gets revenge on her classmates using telekinetic powers. Updates to the material are good and bad, but it’s still an apt, well-acted modern take.
Starring: Summer H. Howell , Samantha Sloyan , Siena Agudong , Alison Thornton
Here’s what critics are saying about Carrie :
Flanagan has created a new take on Carrie White that, while imperfect, is highly addictive. — Nate Richard, Collider
Carrie succeeds in almost every way. — Eric Diaz, Nerdist
Flanagan has done something really special and exciting with Carrie that may not make it the best adaptation (it’s hard to beat De Palma), but something that is breathtakingly audacious in its own right. — Alexander Zalben, Comic Book Club
Considering the magnitude of living up to this legacy, this is a win for Flanagan and King. — Katie Doll, CBR
It probably wasn’t the adaptation of Carrie that I wanted… This Carrie is finally less distinctive and far less scary than it should be. — Daniel Feinberg, The Hollywood Reporter
Carrie simply doesn’t lend itself to a TV approach. Carrie is one of King’s shortest novels, which means any TV series is going to have to stretch the narrative out considerably. — Chris Evangelista, Slashfilm
Carrie has been expanded here with shadings that resemble Firestarter and Needful Things and several other King works, of which even mentioning the name would represent too much of a spoiler. — Daniel Feinberg, The Hollywood Reporter
A more spoiler-filled subplot is filled with nods and references for avid Stephen King and Mike Flanagan fans, and is responsible for some of the most twisted, terrifying moments in the series. — Jordan Williams, Screen Rant
If you’re expecting a faithful take on King’s story, you’ll be sorely disappointed. — Maria Lattila, Film Stories
Mike Flanagan’s eight-episode TV series is bloody terrific, expertly directed and acted, and completely justifies its existence by recontextualizing the classic tale in a modern context. — Alexander Zalben, Comic Book Club
Mike Flanagan’s timely Carrie TV series not only justifies its existence, but compellingly transforms King’s themes and characters into an even more realized, nuanced portrait of the complex intersection of fear, anger, and compassion in society. — Jordan Williams, Screen Rant
Even if Carrie stumbles along the way, it at least makes a solid case for why today’s generation could use a drama like this one. — Saloni Gajjar, AV Club
The new things that Amazon’s Carrie does well don’t make up for the old things that Carrie has always done well and that, unfortunately, aren’t present here. — Daniel Feinberg, The Hollywood Reporter
Mike Flanagan’s Carrie is a topical, timely, and tragic series that takes the core elements of King’s classic novel and reimagines them for today. — Cassondra Feltus, Black Girl Nerds
Flanagan isn’t remaking a classic, but rather giving Carrie a modern makeover befitting our digital age and proving the enduring themes of King’s book. — Saloni Gajjar, AV Club
Carrie 2026 is as much an exploration of what it means to be an outcast in the modern-day world of Instagram as it is about a telekinetic girl who goes on a rampage at prom. — Eric Diaz, Nerdist
Amazon’s Carrie is probably the adaptation of Carrie that 2026 and the current TV landscape deserve, a collection of big authorial choices that are at best admirable and at worst defensible. — Daniel Feinberg, The Hollywood Reporter
Infusing Carrie with modern context could feel issue-driven – and it is; the show is definitely saying a lot about the constant spectre of death our high school students now live under – but it feels par for the “real” teens in the show. — Alexander Zalben, Comic Book Club
It’s a plea instead of a roar, and the modern world, with all its problems, calls for screams. — Ben Travers, IndieWire
Flanagan is appropriately respectful of De Palma’s film, with nods ranging from outright visual homage to the names of several supporting characters to a fleeting glimpse at a movie theater marquee that made me snort aloud. — Daniel Feinberg, The Hollywood Reporter
Wisely, the show acknowledges it right out of the gate and doesn’t pretend the audience is ignorant about what the big climax is… It uses our knowledge to make the journey to that destination surprising and full of mounting tension. — Lauren Sarner, New York Post
This show is not what you think, and at least on this viewer’s end, my jaw dropped when the twists started falling, and every hair on my body stood on end. — Alexander Zalben, Comic Book Club
It honors the original, while tweaking enough details to make it fresh. — Lauren Sarner, New York Post
Margaret White, a one-dimensional and unexplained fundamentalist nightmare on the page and in previous adaptations, becomes a fully explained fundamentalist nightmare here. — Daniel Feinberg, The Hollywood Reporter
To fill out the space of eight 45-minute episodes, the writers invent subplots for supporting characters; Some of them add meaningful twists. — Saloni Gajjar, AV Club
There are also big, unexpected swings here that I must confess left me slightly puzzled. — Chris Evangelista, Slashfilm
Think of the series as Gossip Girl meets X-Men . — Saloni Gajjar, AV Club
What Amazon’s Carrie resembles far more than Carrie is Netflix’s 13 Reasons Why — the good first season, not the two subsequent awful seasons. — Daniel Feinberg, The Hollywood Reporter
It’s less of a slow-burn than his other works but still maintains his exploration of existentialist and spiritual themes. — Nate Richard, Collider
Carrie ‘s prom night is undoubtedly one of the greatest achievements in Flanagan’s career thus far. — Jordan Williams, Screen Rant
For fans of Flanagan’s work, Carrie lands solidly in the middle. It may be underwhelming if you want the Gothic atmosphere and chills of Hill House and Midnight Mass , but it’s better than The Haunting of Bly Manor and The Midnight Club . — Lauren Sarner, New York Post
While Carrie lands closer to The Midnight Club than Midnight Mass in its showrunner’s oeuvre, it makes the most of Flanagan’s mesmeric monologues. — Ben Travers, IndieWire
While there are bursts of horror in Carrie (as you’d expect), the series works best when it finds kinder, more emotional moments for Carrie to grab hold of. — Chris Evangelista, Slashfilm
Carrie is technically a horror series, but there’s a lack of gore and violence featured throughout most of the series. That may sound like a flaw, but it’s a detail that only adds to the emotional experience. — Aaron Pruner, CNET
This [show has] a version of Margaret White you might actually know in real life, which is mildly terrifying. — Eric Diaz, Nerdist
I’ve always found Flanagan far better at building a mood of horror than delivering actual frights, and here even the reliable jump scares don’t have much effect. — Daniel Feinberg, The Hollywood Reporter
Summer H. Howell is something of a revelation… [Her] performance so believable and total that she manages to make the character entirely her own. — Chris Evangelista, Slashfilm
Howell is a revelation in the series, slowly turning from sheltered good girl into something more rounded, occasionally much angrier, but never a full-on monster. — Alexander Zalben, Comic Book Club
She’s more than capable of shifting back and forth between Carrie’s withdrawn moments and the increasing confidence that might come from realizing you can lift objects with your mind. — Daniel Feinberg, The Hollywood Reporter

articles.title_orig: Piep Haus Projects Opens in North Andover with Arthur Henderson’s Hand-Hewn World of Folk Story
articles.title_zh: Piep Haus Projects Opens in North Andover with Arthur Henderson’s Hand-Hewn World of Folk Story
articles.content_orig:
A pie safe, a sausage rope, and a model of the universe are among the curious objects in Peasant’s Burlesque, curated by Stace Brandt.
Quick Bit by Monica Lynn Manoski
Installation view, Arthur Henderson, “Peasant’s Burlesque,” Piep Haus Projects, 2026. Courtesy of Piep House Projects. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
Installation view, Arthur Henderson, “Peasant’s Burlesque,” Piep Haus Projects, 2026. Courtesy of Piep House Projects. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
It was a subtly crisp afternoon with soft light casting long shadows on the curving roads of North Andover as I drove with the windows down to my destination, Piep Haus Projects (PHP), a new experimental pop-up art space hosted at the home of artist Leah Piepgras. I followed a series of hand-painted arrows up the driveway to the far end of a previously shag-carpeted house with the unmistakable vibes of a swingers pad, now transformed into a living space, artist studio, and exhibition room. On my way in, a young person with flowing dark hair snaked past me, weaving in and out of sculptures, down through the yard to the edge of Lake Cochichewick and back through to where I stood.
PHP’s inaugural show features works by Arthur Henderson, a MassArt graduate who now lives and works in “relative isolation” (other than the company of his wife and son) in the woods of Western Connecticut. “Peasant’s Burlesque ,” curated by Stace Brandt, brings together seventeen larger works—all completed since the start of the year—including fourteen sculptures, two woodblock prints, and a Portrait of the Artist at Work in ink on paper, with twenty-two small-scale sculptures housed separately in a cabinet.
Arthur Henderson, Big Red (front), 2026. Plywood, Bondo, paint cabinetry, and plinth with variable objects inside. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
A six-foot-wide wooden chandelier with snuffed candles drew me into the exhibition room in the far end of the house. Titled Model of the Universe from the outside looking in , it’s suspended from the vaulted ceiling with a charcoal-colored chain. The work’s seven distinct arms invite your eyes to return again and again to trace the irregular edges, which, although cut from plywood, have a hand-drawn quality.
​ Big Red (2026), a chestnut-colored pie cabinet with doors splayed, holds a curious accumulation of hand-carved items including a pipe, medicine cup, and a stack of Porterhouse steaks. Its plywood back bears chiseled hands spelling P-I-E-S-A-F-E in American Sign Language. Underneath its four legs, an ebony trap door gives a sense of dark mystery. I found myself imagining who or what is beneath it.
​A glowing ember box serves as a pedestal for a hand-hewn baguette and beer can. Custom-crafted box crates elevate other lovingly shaped objects, including Milkcrib , a four-walled resting place for an imagined gallon of milk, and Decoy (Skull in Repose) , a small sculpture resembling a bruised and tilted three-dimensional heart. Throughout the room things are placed casually—like how you might find a space left if someone weren’t expecting company. On my way out, I passed a staircase guarded by a string of sausage links and a sign marked “Champagne Room,” which made me smile and want to stay and snoop around.
(left) Detail view of objects inside Big Red including Steaks , 2026. (right) Big Red (back), 2026. Plywood, Bondo, paint cabinetry, and plinth. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
The show exudes a whimsical, masculine energy, with each object serving as a breadcrumb to a larger narrative series the artist calls The Feast of the Butcher King . The objects in “Peasant’s Burlesque” are made from the perspective of the townsfolk who fall victim to the Butcher King in a retake on the folktale “Stone Soup.” The viewer enters a “set” where objects are contrived as offerings in exchange for the magic soup stone.
Brandt thoughtfully responded to the challenge of bringing Henderson’s purposely rough-hewn objects together with the newly renovated white cork-floored, multi-windowed project space. Henderson said, “What could’ve created a tension or competition instead feels very harmonious—a true conversation between the objects and their surroundings.”
​Arthur Henderson and Stace Brandt will be present with the work on Sunday, October 25, 2026, from 1:00 to 6:00 p.m. Between now and then, the space is open by appointment. Reach out to leah.piepgras@gmail.com for availability.

articles.title_orig: Fed Minutes Signal Further Rate Increase This Year, but No Urgency for October Hike
articles.title_zh: Fed Minutes Signal Further Rate Increase This Year, but No Urgency for October Hike
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Minutes from the Federal Reserve's September policy meeting reflect unanimous agreement among officials that interest rates needed to be higher to combat persistent inflation.
"Participants generally emphasized that inflation remained elevated while the labor market appeared to be near full employment, with some signs of strengthening, and that economic activity was expanding at a solid pace. Furthermore, almost all participants assessed that, while inflation risks were tilted to the upside, risks to the labor market had diminished and were now broadly balanced," minutes from the Sept. 16 meeting released Wednesday stated.
"Based on the outlook and the changing balance of risks, all participants viewed a higher target range for the federal funds rate as appropriate."
The Fed voted unanimously on Sept. 16 to raise rates, the first hike in three years . And at the time, most Federal Open Market Committee members saw a need for at least one more 25 basis point rate hike this year.
Markets were banking on a hike and expecting more to come.
But economic data released in the past few weeks has changed the picture considerably. "Core" PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose a relatively cool 3% in August , beating expectations for a rise of 3.3% and marking a drop from 3.3% in July. Meanwhile, September jobs numbers fell far short of economists' expectations, with a gain of just 29,000 jobs , while the unemployment rate edged up to 4.2% from 4.1%.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
That less rosy jobs picture, combined with a more positive read on inflation, had analysts — and some Fed officials — throwing cold water on the notion of another rate hike this month.
"This data won't shift the broader decision-making calculus for the Fed as inflation remains the supreme concern," Chris Hodge, chief economist for Natixis, previously told Yahoo Finance. "But with wages lower and the jobs picture a bit less rosy, it certainly decreases the urgency to hike in October (and perhaps December if inflation data cooperates)."
Even before the September job report, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams had already begun to temper expectations for a rate hike later this month . Both struck a more cautious tone than several of their colleagues, acknowledging that inflation has remained too high, but that the central bank should take time to assess whether it's on a downward path.
Williams said that, after raising rates in September, he sees "no need for urgency" and that "we have time to gather more information."
The FOMC meets again Oct. 27-28. Futures markets see only a 17% chance of a rate hike this month, but a roughly 70% chance in December.

articles.title_orig: The Human Link: Computer Science for Today’s Complex World
articles.title_zh: The Human Link: Computer Science for Today’s Complex World
articles.content_orig:
Whitman faculty and students are envisioning the future of computer science—and it’s about human connection
Painting with a sonic palette. Alice Chan ’27 traveled to Singapore with Assistant Professor of Computer Science Jordan Wirfs-Brock to present EchoField at the Association for Computing Machinery’s Designing Interactive Systems conference. Conference-goers were even able to add their own sounds and collaborate on a sonic map of the conference experience.
In a dark room, a vibrant colorscape spills over the floor. With each step you take, the sounds of Tokyo slowly emerge around you—a meandering patchwork of sonic memories corresponding to the swirl of colors at your feet: Ambient noise in a temple is bright white. Clattering wind is pale aqua. Pattering rain is red.
This is EchoField—an immersive, interactive audio archive developed by Alice Chan ’27 as a final project for her Computer Science course, Your Life in Sound (CS-100A), taken in her junior year. The class is taught by Assistant Professor of Computer Science Jordan Wirfs-Brock , who encourages her students to think expansively about how humans interact with sound and how creating digital audio archives can connect people more closely with their experiences.
To create EchoField, Chan uploaded brief sound clips she recorded while studying abroad in Tokyo, pairing each with a color. As she started recording sounds in her life, she realized their power to evoke emotion and memory. “When you explore, you listen to the audio and reflect on what happened back then for yourself,” she says.
Chan, a Davis United World College Scholar from Hong Kong, who is studying Japanese while designing her own major in Human-Computer Interaction, hopes to become a user-experience designer, making technology easier for people to use.
EchoField came from her desire to create an app where users could immerse themselves in—and share—the sounds of daily life. She’d learned some coding skills in past classes, but used “vibe coding,” or collaborating with an AI program to write code, to create the first version of EchoField.
I feel like technology has helped me build connections in many ways. I believe in its potential to create even more connection.
Wirfs-Brock was impressed with Chan’s concept and enthusiasm and invited her to work together to refine EchoField and submit a paper about it to conferences. They teamed up with William Bares , Associate Professor of Computer Science, who specializes in designing interactive experiences using motion tracking.
The group helped EchoField leap off the computer screen and into the physical world. Using motion-capture technology, people can now explore a projected image of the colorful archive as audio fills the air, “being in the sound instead of just listening to it,” Chan says.
In June 2026, Chan and Wirfs-Brock presented EchoField to technology researchers from around the world at the Association for Computing Machinery’s Designing Interactive Systems conference in Singapore.
Chan says Whitman has given her the opportunity to study many aspects of how humans interact with technology, including courses in Computer Science, Psychology , Human-Centered Design and Sociology . She believes that technology is important for bringing people together in a global society, where we’re often far apart.
“I feel like technology has helped me build connections in many ways,” she says. “I believe in its potential to create even more connection.”
Play with a sonic palette of sounds recorded in Walla Walla and Singapore. Try it now. Click on the library icon to start exploring sounds recorded around campus, at the Designing Interactive Systems conference and beyond.
‘They want to change the world.’ Today’s Whitman students are searching for innovative ways to harness computer science in the service of humanity, says Chair and Associate Professor of Computer Science William Bares. And the department is evolving to give them the skills to do it.
The values embodied in Chan’s project—human innovation, creativity and empathy—will always be an essential part of computer science, Bares says.
As Chair of Whitman’s Computer Science Department, Bares envisions an inter­disciplinary future where computer scientists and experts in other fields come together, sometimes in collaboration with artificial intelligence, to discover the ideas that AI can’t come up with on its own.
“Creative ideas, entrepreneurial ideas, often come from thinking about a problem from a different perspective, being familiar with different fields,” he says.
Bares and his colleagues in the Computer Science Department are working to design a flexible curriculum that allows students to incorporate ideas from different disciplines and be more adaptable in the face of rapid changes in the computing world.
By leaning into its liberal arts mission, Whitman can help Computer Science students broaden and deepen their skills in ethics, philosophy, communication, critical thinking and human-centered design, Bares says.
Those fundamentally human skills give graduates an edge in a tech industry where traditional career paths are increasingly being reshaped by generative AI.
By providing more opportunities to create projects like EchoField, Whitman can help students build a portfolio that showcases their ability to create impactful work about meaning­ful topics.
“Liberal arts colleges are really positioned perfectly to engage with the future,” Bares says. “These are skills that build multiple pathways for students, so they’ve got that ability to be flexible, which is what the current market demands.”
Liberal arts colleges are really positioned perfectly to engage with the future.
—William Bares, Chair and Associate Professor of Computer Science
Bares compares traditional computer science courses to a single-crop field: focused on one subject, such as data structures, without much cross-pollination.
His vision for Whitman’s Computer Science program is to make space for classes that he compares to meadows: intricate and diverse, drawing in other disciplines the way an abundant landscape attracts and energizes wildlife.
Introductory-level classes like Your Life in Sound innovate by giving students an early opportunity to be creative and imagine pathways to research and entrepreneurship beyond the traditional software developer role, Bares says.
In summer 2024, the faculty met to rewrite the department’s learning outcomes and begin reshaping course offerings and requirements. The updated curriculum emphasizes communication, collaboration and self-directed learning, as well as critical evaluation of computational technologies—considering whether technologies are efficient and ethical and thinking about the impact they have on society, communities and environments.
Bares says this work is inspired by students’ passionate interest in making the world better. “They want to do positive things for the environment, they want to help people, they want to know that what they’re learning and doing has a benefit.”
Some of the new courses and requirements have already been rolled out, and much like product testing, the department is gathering student feedback so that faculty can continue to improve their course offerings and teaching.
Bares hopes that the next iteration of the Computer Science curriculum will make room for even more courses like Your Life in Sound and innovative senior capstone projects, such as interactive data installations, independent research and startup launches.
In concert with interdisciplinary classes, Bares also dreams of creating more opportunities for students to showcase their projects to the campus community and the public—and he envisions larger, more accessible spaces for these immersive experiences on campus.
“This is the future of computer science,” Bares says. “We believe this is going to be what will excite students to want to come here, and also faculty to want to come here and be part of this.”
