This latest solo play is the third in Moran's trilogy, following The Tricky Part and All the Rage .
October 07, 2026 By Logan Culwell-Block
Other Bodies , a new solo play from Martin Moran , will make its world premiere Off-Broadway via Barrow Group, with performances beginning November 19 ahead of a November 23 opening night.
The work is the third in Moran's trilogy of solo works, following the 2004 Obie-winning The Tricky Part and 2013's Lucille Lortel Award-winning All the Rage . As with the earlier works, Seth Barrish is directing.
“For more than 20 years, these solo pieces have been a way for me to wrestle with questions I don’t know how to answer,” shares Moran in a statement. “ Other Bodies grew out of the pandemic, a moment when we were suddenly forced apart from one another, but it became an exploration of something much larger: how we live with difference, how we recognize experiences that aren’t our own, and how we find our way back to one another. I didn’t set out to write a trilogy, but returning to this form with Seth, and bringing this third piece to The Barrow Group, where The Tricky Part first began, feels like completing a circle.”
Moran's Broadway credits include roles in Spamalot , Cabaret , Titanic , Wicked , Big River , and Funny Girl , along with the Off-Broadway premiere of Floyd Collins .
Tickets are at BarrowGroup.org .

articles.title_orig: Why Trump just loosened the rules on 'dyed diesel' — normally a farm fuel
articles.title_zh: Why Trump just loosened the rules on 'dyed diesel' — normally a farm fuel
articles.content_orig:
In this aerial view, Dan Duffy uses a tractor to plant soybeans on land he farms with his brother on April 28, 2025 near Dwight, Illinois. Scott Olson/Getty Images North America hide caption
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Less than a month before the midterms, the price of fuel is becoming a powerful election issue .
This week, President Trump issued an executive order aimed at lowering costs for frequent diesel users by making a type of fuel called "dyed diesel" more accessible through the end of the year.
Could this lower the cost of diesel? Let's get into it.
Why is diesel so expensive right now?
Prices for all kinds of oil products have risen this year because fewer ships have been getting through the Strait of Hormuz and transporting crude to refineries worldwide — but the diesel supply chain has been uniquely hit. Ukraine's recent attacks on Russian refineries have taken many of them offline, and Russia has cut back on its diesel exports. China has, too.
It's added up to a limited supply of diesel — a fuel that powers much of the industrial supply chain.
So its price has soared; the U.S. average for a gallon hit a record of $6.52 a few weeks ago. The price has eased a bit since then, but a gallon remains about $2.60 higher than this time last year, according to AAA .
When diesel prices rise, inflation is likely to follow, analysts say. Diesel powers much of the industrial supply chain, from agricultural equipment to trucks transporting goods from warehouses to grocery stores.
The "dyed" part means: red dye. "Red-dyed diesel is diesel with red dye in it. That's it," said Will O'Neill, principal analyst at S&P Global Energy and a follower of all things diesel.
Chemically, this diesel is almost identical to the regular kind you'd find in most gas stations. But it's a different color because it's used, and taxed, differently.
Red-dyed diesel is only meant for off-road vehicles, mainly farm and construction equipment — like a tractor that's used in a field. It's exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon on commercial diesel.
Drivers aren't suppose to use it in vehicles that drive on highways. People who do are subject to an IRS penalty — either $1,000 or $10 per gallon, whichever is more expensive.
The red color makes it easier to catch someone who filled up their tank with the wrong stuff. Using the red-dyed diesel is "effectively a form of tax evasion," O'Neill said.
But the new executive order says dyed diesel will be allowed on highways through the end of the year. The IRS won't penalize anyone who uses it.
Will this save people money?
It could help farmers, truckers and other workers who count on diesel to do their jobs. The executive order said this move would put money directly into their pockets "to support their vital service to our Nation."
It essentially expands the ways in which workers can use dyed diesel, sparing them the federal tax. Imagine a farmer who usually puts dyed diesel in their tractor — now they can also legally use it to fill up their cargo van, get on the highway, and take their produce to market.
Plus, a handful of states have said drivers can use red-dyed diesel on their highways. On average , state diesel taxes run about 35 cents a gallon. Allowing drivers to use dyed diesel — and skip both federal and state taxes — could add up to a savings of about 60 cents a gallon.
But because the cost of a gallon of regular diesel is now about $2.60 higher than this time last year, drivers will still be paying a higher price overall
Will this put more diesel on the market?
Technically, this will increase the total amount of diesel that people could use.
But Jaime Brito, executive director of oil markets at Dow Jones Energy, points out that this doesn't mean most people can easily access dyed diesel. It isn't available at most gas stations. "When was the last time that you went to a pumping station and you saw that one of the stations gave you the possibility to feed red diesel into your truck?" he asked.
Instead, people would need to go to a special wholesaler — or might be able to find it at gas stations in rural areas.
In an email to NPR responding to these critiques, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers wrote that the president wants to see prices fall and is taking "historic measures" to alleviate oil supply disruptions.
Can the Trump administration do anything else to lower diesel costs?
Over the past month, some politicians have floated the idea of a diesel export ban . The idea was that if the U.S. stopped sending diesel to other countries, maybe that would temporarily increase the supply in the U.S., pushing down the price.
But bottom line: refiners pushed back . It would be bad business for them.
Refiners make money by selling diesel within the U.S. and exporting it around the world, said Jacques Rousseau, who focuses on  oil, natural gas, and refined products as  a managing director with Clearview Energy Partners.
If there was a diesel export ban, sure, that diesel would stay in the U.S. But then, refineries would wind up with a ton of extra diesel. "Then it'll start going into storage. And then once your storage gets filled, then you have to reduce the overall production of your refinery. So then you just start producing less of everything else too because you have nowhere to put this diesel," Rousseau said.
Ultimately, that could lead to prices for refined oil products, like gasoline — and diesel — going up .
President Trump said late Friday that he was not seriously considering an export ban , and that the U.S. didn't need one anymore, as Europe just released about 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from its own stockpiles.
Analysts told NPR that the only real fix will be ending the wars in Iran and Ukraine — until there's more oil flowing freely around the world again, they said, it's hard to see the price of diesel getting much lower. " There's no silver bullet," said O'Neill. "There's no way to snap your fingers and end up with $4 diesel before the election."
"Barring the rapid and credible conclusion of the wars," he continued, "I don't think that happens."

articles.title_orig: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.title_zh: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.content_orig:
Tulane Law School’s longstanding strength in comparative law was on full display in Berlin, where four faculty members took on prominent scholarly roles at one of the world’s most important gatherings of comparative law experts.
Tulane professors Vernon Valentine Palmer, James Gordley, Ronald J. Scalise Jr. and Mateusz Grochowski served as reporters at the 22nd General Congress of the International Academy of Comparative Law, held Sept. 28-Oct. 2 at Humboldt University of Berlin. Tulane faculty had the largest delegation and produced more reports for the gathering than faculty from any other U.S. law school.
Their roles included some of the congress’ most significant scholarly assignments. Palmer served as a general reporter, bringing together reports from 19 countries, while Gordley served as a special reporter. Scalise and Grochowski each represented the United States as national reporters on separate topics.
The strong showing is indicative of Tulane Law’s unique place in comparative and civil law scholarship, a tradition rooted in Louisiana’s mixed legal system and sustained by generations of internationally recognized scholars.
The International Academy of Comparative Law, founded in 1924, brings together leading scholars from legal systems around the world. Its General Congress is held every four years and has been described as the “World Congress of Law,” drawing roughly 1,000 scholars from more than 70 countries to Berlin this year.
Palmer, the Thomas Pickles Professor of Law and a globally recognized authority on mixed legal systems, served as general reporter for “Mixed Jurisdictions and Mixed Legal Systems from Around the World.” In that leadership role, Palmer synthesized 19 individual country reports examining the distinctive mix of legal traditions within each system.
Gordley, the W.R. Irby Distinguished University Research Professor, served as a special reporter for a panel examining “Contractual Fairness in the Rebirth of an Idea.” His report explored the distinction between an unfair contract and a “bad bargain,” and how legal systems around the world determine where one ends and the other begins.
Scalise, the Eason-Weinmann Chair in International and Comparative Law, served as a U.S. national reporter on “Trusts in Non-Common Law Systems,” examining the subject through both U.S. and Louisiana perspectives.
Grochowski also represented the United States as a national reporter, addressing “Innovative Complements and Substitutes for Contracts” and examining emerging alternatives to traditional contractual relationships in American law.
The reports by Tulane faculty, along with those of other U.S. scholars participating in the congress, are published in the American Journal of Comparative Law , one of the leading journals in the field.
Tulane’s influence extended beyond the congress’ scholarly program.
The Berlin gathering coincided with the annual meeting of the American Society of Comparative Law, the leading U.S. organization devoted to the comparative study of legal systems and traditions. Two Tulane professors hold leadership positions in the organization: Scalise serves as treasurer and Sally Brown Richardson, the A.D. Freeman Professor of Civil Law, serves as parliamentarian. Both helped lead the society’s business meeting in Berlin.
Tulane’s leadership in the field will come home to New Orleans next year.
In fall 2027, Tulane Law will host the American Society of Comparative Law’s annual conference, bringing more than 100 comparative law scholars from around the world to the law school for a three-day examination of “The Role of Comparative Law in a Global (and Sometimes Anti-Global) World.”
The gathering will put Tulane at the center of an international scholarly conversation that has long been part of the law school’s identity, and one in which its faculty continue to play leading roles.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) is investigating reports of a second possible pneumonic plague case in Siberia after the death of a laboratory worker who was allegedly exposed to the illness.
Global health officials are pushing Moscow for transparency following the death of 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov.
Shipilova was admitted to hospital late last month with acute respiratory failure and placed on a ventilator before passing away on 2 October.
Local media reported that she was exposed to a dangerous pathogen after accidentally shattering a sample tube during routine laboratory work.
But senior Russian epidemiologist Mikhail Favorov cast doubt on that account in comments to The Moscow Times earlier this week, pointing out that personnel at the institute operate in full protective suits.
"It's laughable," Favorov said. "If you break a test tube, the likelihood of infection is actually very low. In short, it doesn't matter to the general public – they'll believe the 'broken test tube' story."
"It's absolutely hair-raising," he added. "We will not be told what really happened."
Independent regional news outlet Lyudi Baikal reported that a second individual with symptoms of severe pulmonary distress had died at an Irkutsk regional medical facility. The report has not been independently verified.
At least 197 people identified as direct or indirect contacts of the laboratory staff remain under medical isolation, with around 100 currently being monitored in hospital wards.
WHO director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus confirmed that the UN agency has requested additional information from Russian health authorities regarding a second employee presenting with unexplained pneumonia.
In a statement released late on Tuesday, Dr Ghebreyesus pushed for Russia to release all known information about the outbreak: “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
But so far, official statements have appeared contradictory .
While municipal authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk posted a warning on Telegram urging residents to avoid traveling to Shelekhov, the message was removed from the official channel two hours later, according to Lyudi Baikal .
Alexey Tsydenov, head of the neighbouring Republic of Buryatia, also initially shared on social media that the technician had died of plague, before editing his post to state she "may have" been infected.
The conflicting official accounts have heightened concerns surrounding the disease. Regional outlets report that Shipilova worked with the bacterium Yersinia pestis – the same behind the “ Black Death ” that wiped out more than a third of Europe’s population in the 14th century.
Moscow has informed the WHO that an epidemiological investigation has been completed and claims that testing has detected no high-threat pathogens among monitored contacts.
Unlike bubonic plague, which is transmitted through flea bites, pneumonic plague infects the lungs directly and can spread rapidly between humans via airborne respiratory droplets.
The WHO has stated that it remains in close contact with Russian authorities and has offered technical support to manage and contain any potential outbreak.

Doc is one of only two B-29s still flying today. More than 1,600 were built in Wichita during the war.
It is joined by a P-51 Mustang. Those are rare too. Only about 150 of them are still around.
Visitors got a chance to see the aircraft up close and learn about the crews who designed, built and flew them.
“It’s a pretty special opportunity...really makes the history jump off the page,” Josh Wells said.
Wells said the event also helps younger generations understand an important piece of history.

articles.title_orig: How PvP Progression in World of Warcraft: Forever Works
articles.title_zh: How PvP Progression in World of Warcraft: Forever Works
articles.content_orig:
Whether you’re charging into battlegrounds with your faction or setting your sights on long-term PvP (Player vs. Player) goals, World of Warcraft: Forever brings a refreshed sense of purpose to every match-up. This approach gives players more reasons to take part throughout the season while preserving the spirit of competition that defined PvP in the original World of Warcraft .
When reimagining the PvP system, we wanted to keep the design pillar of “Approachable and Familiar” firmly in view: simplifying the original Honor System while staying true to its roots.
In World of Warcraft: Forever, PvP progression has two parts: Honor and Rank Points.
Honor is a currency players earn through taking part in PvP content. This includes defeating other players, completing battlegrounds, and finishing relevant PvP quests. Players also earn increased Honor in highlighted battlegrounds during their holiday weeks.
As part of these updates, we reviewed Honor gains across battlegrounds so acquisition rates are more consistent across the board. We want players to enjoy the full range of battleground maps without feeling compelled to choose Alterac Valley solely for Honor efficiency.
Rank Points come from PvP activities such as battlegrounds and relevant PvP quests, with holiday-week battlegrounds offering an additional boost. As players earn Rank Points, they advance through familiar PvP ranks from original World of Warcraft, working toward the ultimate titles of High Warlord for the Horde or Grand Marshal for the Alliance. Ranks have a weekly cap, retaining the foundation of the original system while making the journey more accessible.
Honor can be used to purchase two sets of PvP gear: one blue-quality set and one epic-quality set. The epic set requires the blue piece plus an Emboldened Seal to upgrade it, and Emboldened Seals have rank requirements players must reach before purchasing. There are also new and reworked items to fill gaps for specializations that were previously missing options. For example, Shaman now have healer, melee, and caster PvP gear sets they can acquire.
Below are the rank requirements for PvP item rewards:
Rank 1 - Tabard Rank 2 - PvP Trinket Rank 3 - Cloaks Rank 4 - Necklace Rank 5 - Combat Potions Rank 6 - Tabard Rank 7 - Battle Standard Rank 8 - Epic Bracers/Epic Belt Upgrade Token Rank 9 - Epic Boots Upgrade Token Rank 10 - Epic Gloves Upgrade Token Rank 11 - Mounts Rank 12 - Epic Legs/Epic Shoulders Upgrade Token Rank 13 - Epic Chest/Epic Helm Upgrade Token Rank 14 - Epic Weapons
To view your progress, you can open your Character Pane (Hotkey-C) then select the Player vs. Player tab on the right side of the interface. It will show you your rank, your current Rank Points, and what rewards are available for purchase based on your rank.
During a PvP season, players can progress through the ranks and earn Honor. Each season also includes a journey with weekly tasks to complete. Successfully completing those tasks grants Honor and Rank Points, and three tasks each season also grant a Legacy Point. Completing these tasks is part of the seasonal journey, and because they are tied to the Legacy System, they remain available to complete in future seasons.
With more ways to make progress each week and meaningful goals to pursue throughout the season, PvP in World of Warcraft: Forever gives players a clear path to jump in, compete, and keep building toward what comes next.

Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and U.S. President Donald Trump are seen in this combination of pictures created on Dec. 2, 2025.
President Donald Trump on Thursday said he is following the upcoming Brazilian election “very closely,” referring to Brazil as a “very important" country. "The people of Brazil are fantastic people,” he told reporters outside the White House. “It’s a very important election.”
The U.S. State Department later announced the suspension of its consular services in Brazil ahead of the election taking place on Sunday, citing unspecified security concerns. “U.S. citizens seeking emergency assistance during this time should not come to the Embassy, the Consulates, or other U.S. diplomatic facilities,” the security alert advised.
Brazilians are heading to the polls for a set of federal elections spanning congressional and gubernatorial races, alongside the first round of the presidential election votes. It’s set to be a decisive moment for Latin America’s largest nation, as the region has seen a shift toward the right in recent years. An Oct. 25 runoff is expected, as polls show a tight contest between leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro , who was convicted last year for plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 election loss. Trump led the conservative voices denouncing the conviction, referring to the trial as a “ witch hunt .”
While Trump has acknowledged his active interest as Brazil votes on its political future, there are concerns he could be too involved. Trump and his Administration have been accused of attempting to interfere with the high-stakes overseas election.
In a letter sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio in late September, Democratic lawmakers expressed “grave concern” over what they referred to as “the Administration’s coordinated effort to threaten our strategic alliance with Brazil and undermine the Western Hemisphere’s second-largest democracy ahead of its upcoming presidential election.”
“Over the course of President Trump’s second term, we have seen U.S. officials engage in a sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil,” the lawmakers said in the Sept. 24 letter, signed by 30 House Democrats and Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who caucuses with the Democratic Party.
In another letter sent to Rubio on Monday, three Democratic Senators voiced similar concerns about potential U.S. interference.
“This effort first escalated sharply during the summer of 2025, with the [U.S.] Administration deploying tariffs and targeted sanctions to attempt to shape the Brazilian Supreme Court’s verdict in the trial of former President Jair Bolsonaro on charges of attempting to foment a military coup to stay in power,” said the Senators, noting that the tariff pressure escalated in July this year when the Trump Administration moved to impose a new 25% tariff on many imports from Brazil—a decision labeled a “lamentable milestone” by Lula’s office.
The Senators argued that the “campaign directed at Brazil’s authorities resumed with the appointment of Darren Beattie as a senior advisor on Brazil issues in the State Department.” Beattie served as a White House speech writer in Trump’s first term, but was axed for attending a gathering of white supremacists. He returned to the fold early on in Trump’s second term. When serving as undersecretary for public diplomacy and public affairs last year, he called one of Brazil’s Supreme Court Judges a “key architect of the censorship and persecution complex directed against Bolsonaro and his supporters.”
Accusing the Trump Administration of using “diplomatic, economic, and political pressure in ways that risk weakening [Brazil’s] democratic institutions [and] undermining confidence in Brazil's electoral process,” the Senators closed the letter by asking the Administration to “commit to recognizing the certified outcome of Brazil's 2026 democratic elections.”
The White House has staunchly rejected claims of interference in Brazil’s elections.
“Conservative leaders are winning elections across the Western Hemisphere on their own merit because everyone sees the success of President Trump’s policies,” said White House spokesperson Anna Kelly in a statement to TIME. “These claims are nonsense.”
President Lula has also expressed concern over Trump’s interest in his country’s election. “I have already told President Trump it is very important that the U.S. do not interfere in Brazil’s elections,” he said in a Sept. 22 interview. “Brazilian elections are the concern of the Brazilian people. American elections are the concern of the American people.”
Lula added that he is “very worried about Marco Rubio,” claiming that the U.S. Secretary of State “is very closely connected to Bolsonaro’s people,” though he stressed that this was only “suspicion.” TIME has reached out to the State Department for comment.
Trump has not formally endorsed either candidate in Brazil’s presidential race, but his defense of former Brazilian President Bolsonaro, who was last year sentenced to 27 years in prison, is well documented.
After Trump criticized the trial proceedings as a “terrible thing” in July 2025, the Trump Administration increased pressure on Brazil’s government by imposing punishing 50% tariffs— extended in part due to Bolsonaro’s treatment in the courts—and directing the office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) to investigate trade relations with the country.
The State Department added to the pressure later that same month, when Rubio called Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes’ actions a “political witch hunt against Jair Bolsonaro” and announced visa restrictions on Moraes, unspecified judicial allies, and their immediate families.
Feliciano de Sá Guimarães, an associate professor at the Institute of International Relations at the University of São Paulo, says Lula was able to turn the economic pressure into a political argument of his own.
“Lula realized that he could play [these threats] in his favor for electoral purposes,” he says, explaining that Lula used the concept of “ rally round the flag ,” meaning that once a country is targeted by another, “the incumbent President can rally the people and say, ‘look our sovereignty is under attack.’”
The theme of sovereignty has featured prominently in Lula’s 2026 government manifesto , which points to Trump’s tariffs as damaging the Brazilian economy.
Guimarães says the U.S. Administration has since slightly altered its strategy, favoring an approach that could instead benefit Lula’s opposition.
Flávio Bolsonaro met with Trump, Rubio, and Vice President J.D. Vance at the White House in May. Trump later described the Brazilian lawmaker as a “smart young man, who loves his country very much.” Shortly after that meeting, the U.S. Administration on May 28 designated Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho—two Brazilian gangs—as terrorist organizations, with Bolsonaro appearing to take credit for the move in the media.
Guimarães says the issue may have resonated in Brazil due to public concerns about crime.
“Brazilians are so desperate with the situation of crime in the country that they are resorting to support any initiative, whether it's coming from the federal government or a foreign power to fix the problem,” Guimarães explains, so the move could be seen to strengthen Bolsonaro’s chances with the electorate.
Economic pressure has continued as well. After ordering the USTR to investigate Brazil’s trade practices last year, the office imposed 25% tariffs on the country in July under Section 301, for what it described as unfair trade practices.

articles.title_orig: Merz’s conservatives in new crisis over alleged support for AfD
articles.title_zh: Merz’s conservatives in new crisis over alleged support for AfD
articles.content_orig:
Following events in the parliament of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday, speculation is rife that lawmakers from the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) helped elect a far-right extremist as parliamentary speaker.
This would not only violate prior internal agreements, but also come despite the insistence of CDU Chairman, Chancellor Friedrich Merz , that his party would not cooperate with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) anywhere.
In the first session of the parliament in Magdeburg , the capital of Saxony-Anhalt, following the AfD's election victory on September 6, Tobias Rausch was elected parliamentary speaker — the first time a representative of a far-right party had held such a position since the end of World War II .
Rausch was backed by his own party and the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Rationality (BSW), formerly known as the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, as had been expected.  However, he also received four additional votes by secret ballot. Most observers believe these votes could only have come from right-wing CDU lawmakers.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Leading members of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) were quick to take to the streets in protest in Berlin on Tuesday, marching from the Bundestag through the Brandenburg Gate to nearby Bebelplatz — the very spot where, in 1933, the Nazis burned books by authors they deemed unacceptable. The march concluded with SPD Federal Minister of Defense Boris Pistorius leading the crowd in the German national anthem. Many participants displayed copies of the German Basic Law , a symbol of democracy to stand up for the rule of law and the constitution.
Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil (SPD) summarized the situation, "Electing far-right extremists to such an office represents a taboo brake. Not only the BSW, but also the CDU must urgently explain how this could have happened." Klingbeil's SPD is, after all, the junior coalition partner in the federal government.
The events in Magdeburg thus also cast a shadow over the governing coalition.
It didn't help much that the leader of the CDU parliamentary group, Thorsten Frei, was careful in his wording.
"It's a secret ballot, so of course, in principle, anybody is suspect." he said. He also added, "The fact that this happened is, in my view, extremely troubling and cause for concern."
The result of the first election in the new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt thus offers only a glimpse of the fierce debates to come on how to deal with the AfD. The far-right party won 44% of the vote after having campaigned on extremely tough immigration policies, climate change denial and calls for the near-total abolition of public broadcasting.
Despite its election victory, the AfD does not have a parliamentary majority on its own. In the small eastern state, the regional branch of the party has been classified by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution as "confirmed right-wing extremist."
So once again, the debate about the "firewall" returns. The term refers to the stance taken by democratic parties of ruling out any form of cooperation with the AfD.
At the city and municipal levels, this approach has long since stopped working. Many political analysts have pointed out that the "firewall" has not benefited the CDU, but cooperating with the AfD is also seen as a slippery slope.
Georg Maier, the SPD Interior Minister of the state of Thuringia , agrees. "If the CDU continues down this path, it will contribute to its own downfall. The firewall does serve a purpose."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
BSW co-leader Fabio De Masi told the Hamburger Abendblatt newspaper, "We have to pull the AfD out from behind the firewall. Until now, it hasn't had to prove anything and has been able to conceal its internal contradictions. I don't want the AfD to continue growing behind the firewall."
The BSW, a party founded by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht that has retained some left-wing positions while also aligning itself with the AfD on social issues, paved the way for Rausch's election as parliamentary speaker when it announced that it would vote for him.
The BSW barely managed to cross the 5% threshold for representation in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament. How closely its five MPs want to work with the AfD in the future remains to be seen.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
AfD caucus leader Oliver Kirchner recently expressed criticism of BSW co-leaders De Masi and Mohamed Ali, who both have an immigrant background.
"Am I now supposed to spend five years in politics with people who are under the leadership of Mohamed Ali and this half-Italian guy who says, 'They're all Nazis'?" Kirchner told the right-wing magazine Compact earlier this month.
Up until now, support from the BSW has been seen as the AfD's only real chance of coming to power in Saxony-Anhalt. The other parties — the CDU, the SPD, the Greens and the Left Party — continue to categorically rule out any cooperation with the AfD. Whether that will remain the case in the coming weeks is now the big question.

articles.content_orig:
ATHENS — Georgia coach Kirby Smart is keeping his focus on the Alabama game — not the weather — as Saturday’s showdown in Tuscaloosa approaches.
Tropical Storm Isaias is heading toward the gulf coast, and WALA-Mobile is reporting it is forecast to strengthen to a hurricane on Thursday.
The National Hurricane Center is forecasting the system to turn toward the north on Friday and has projections indicating the path of the storm might reach Tuscaloosa.
Georgia is scheduled to play at Alabama in Bryant-Denny Stadium at 7:30 p.m. on Saturday.
“It’s certainly beyond my control, so we as coaches game plan for multiple situations for weather conditions when they’re there,” Smart said. “We had the same prep last week with the threat of those things, so (it) doesn’t change a lot about practice.”
Heavy rains and wind were originally forecast for Georgia’s home game with Vanderbilt last Saturday, but the storms did not come to pass.
Smart said the same staples apply to each practice week.
“You still have good on good, you’ve got to practice for the long term of the season, not just one week,” Smart said. “You can’t really practice conditions, you can’t simulate them, so you’re much better to educate (and) learn from the past of other people that have played in them and prepare your team to play and not make it about that.”
Smart said he has and will continue to get updates on the projected weather.
“I’m focused on trying to prepare our team, and game plan, and scheme, and all of those things,” Smart said. “I have an update, and they keep m updated with what’s going on (with) meetings, decisions, the way things are leaning and things like that.”
Smart said he does not have any input on any decisions that might be made about the scheduling of the game, and he is not aware of any timeline associated with possible changes.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI says teens use ChatGPT for under 15 minutes a day as worries over risks grow
articles.title_zh: OpenAI says teens use ChatGPT for under 15 minutes a day as worries over risks grow
articles.content_orig:
College Planner is coming to ChatGPT for teens, alongside a new teen AI council and more tools for learning.
Since we introduced ChatGPT for Teens —the default experience automatically applied to accounts identified as under 18—we’ve seen young people use it to learn, explore ideas and solve everyday problems. Today, we’re sharing early progress on ChatGPT for Teens, including how teens are using its learning tools, along with new ways for teens to study and prepare for college.
ChatGPT’s 1.2 billion users span many countries, communities and backgrounds. That reach makes it especially important to build tools that help young people with different resources and opportunities learn and prepare for their futures.
ChatGPT for Teens is designed to help young people learn, think critically and deepen their understanding. As ChatGPT for Teens became available to more teens globally, those with access sent about 2.7 million more learning-related messages on average than those who didn’t have it yet.
Once enrolled, teens use ChatGPT for Teens’ learning tools at scale. The most selected conversation starter prompts are “ask questions to develop my ideas,” “give feedback on my draft,” and “help me check my evidence.” In one week, nearly 1.2 million teens used Learning Visualizations to better understand math and science concepts, and more than 180,000 used Study Mode for step-by-step learning support.
ChatGPT for Teens includes built-in reminders to encourage teens to take breaks. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT. While less than 2% of teens spend more than three consecutive hours on ChatGPT, in almost half of teen conversations with a break reminder, teens took a break or ended their conversation within five minutes. These usage patterns remain well below the publicly reported ⁠ (opens in a new window) average of 5 hours for teen social media usage, and reflect a different kind of experience: ChatGPT is designed for learning, building, and creativity, rather than passive scrolling. Among teens with sessions longer than three consecutive hours, over 80% had at least one prompt related to learning.
These early signs are encouraging and we’ll continue to evaluate the experience and learn from teens, families and educators to improve ChatGPT for Teens.
Hundreds of thousands of US teens use ChatGPT each week to plan for college. They’re using it to plan applications, track deadlines, research schools and understand financial aid.
That’s why we’ll soon be adding College Planner to ChatGPT for Teens. We’re designing it to help students manage the practical steps of applying to college, without taking over the personal work of figuring out where they want to apply. Students have different levels of access to support with college applications. Our goal is to make help more accessible, regardless of financial circumstances, alongside guidance from counselors, advisers, and families.
College Planner brings together application requirements, deadlines, tasks, and financial-aid steps for schools on a student’s list in one plan. Students applying to several colleges can return to it to update their progress, use the timeline to plan ahead and see what’s left to do. They can also ask ChatGPT questions along the way, from what a requirement means to how to get started. By bringing these steps together, we aim to save students and families time and make a stressful process feel more manageable.
We’re designing the initial US experience for high-school students in grades 10–12 who are planning to attend a four-year college. We plan to bring College Planner to students in more countries and expand support to two-year colleges, technical colleges, trade schools and more over time.
College Planner also helps students figure out how to pay for college. They can get help understanding financial aid requirements, track each school’s aid deadlines, and explore scholarships and fee waivers.
Keeping track of an application is only one part of preparing for college. Many students also need someone to help them make sense of their options. Alongside College Planner, we’re supporting College Advising Corps ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a nonprofit that places recent college graduates as advisers in under-resourced high schools to help students navigate the path to higher education. OpenAI’s contribution will help the organization expand into new states and create an AI fellowship program. Through the fellowship, advisers across participating states will test and share practical ways to use AI to help more students navigate the path to college. AI can help students manage application and enrollment tasks. Advisers can help them consider their options and decide what to do next.
When we introduced ChatGPT for Teens , we committed to keep improving the experience. We’re supporting Boston Children’s Hospital’s Digital Wellness Lab ⁠ (opens in a new window) and its independent Student Advisory Council ⁠ (opens in a new window) over the next three years to learn directly from young people about how AI fits into their lives and to give teenagers a meaningful stake at the table as AI is being designed.
For the 2026–27 school year, the Lab will bring together ~22 students across two tracks: ~12 students ages 14–18 working on digital wellbeing projects in their communities and ~10 students ages 16–20, focused on building AI chatbots and emerging technology. These students will work alongside researchers and clinicians on digital wellbeing and AI projects. Students in the AI track will test tools and recommend changes based on how they use AI in learning and their personal lives. We expect to seek feedback on teen safety defaults, parental controls and notifications and AI literacy.
Teens should play a central role in developing the tools that will shape their future. Teens will test tools and develop recommendations for the people building them. Our aim is to bring those recommendations into product and model decisions early and to report back to students on what we change and why. This advisory board will give them a direct voice in that work and share their insights and recommendations to help the wider industry build better tools for young people.
We heard from students that photographing and uploading their notes to ChatGPT can take hours. We’re making it easier for students to turn their notes into study materials like flashcards and quizzes.
With continuous, multi-photo capture, students can photograph multiple pages of notes and automatically combine them into a single PDF, ready to upload to ChatGPT. This is available on iOS, and we’re working to bring it to Android.
We’re also adding flashcards to help teens practice what they’re learning. A student preparing for a biology test, for example, can upload class notes or choose a topic, and ChatGPT can turn the material into cards to review. They can mark the cards they know, return to the ones they missed or shuffle the deck for another round. Decks are saved in a teen’s Library, so it’s easy to pick up where they left off. Students can also ask ChatGPT to pull up the flashcards and create a scheduled task to practice them.
Alongside flashcards, we’ve made it easier to create Quizzes in ChatGPT. Students can now upload their notes to turn them into interactive quizzes, and ChatGPT is better at recognizing when you want a quiz and creating one directly in chat.
We’ll keep learning from teens, families and educators, checking how protections work in practice and sharing what we learn as ChatGPT for Teens evolves.

articles.title_orig: Trump claims world’s lowest drug prices. TrumpRx discounts are a ‘mixed bag,’ report shows.
articles.title_zh: Trump claims world’s lowest drug prices. TrumpRx discounts are a ‘mixed bag,’ report shows.
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, President Donald Trump has increasingly touted his drug pricing deals, claiming the U.S. is now paying the world’s lowest prescription drug prices. “This one thing alone should win us the midterms,” he recently said at the White House.
TrumpRx.gov, the public face of his drug pricing discounts, has grown dramatically since its launch in February. What started as a few dozen brand-name drugs now includes a catalog of more than 800 brand-name and generic medications, offering discounts on everything from popular weight loss drugs to treatments for cancer and rheumatoid arthritis.
It’s unclear whether the average American has “ saved a fortune,” as Trump promised .
Prescription drug prices fell by 3.1% over the year ending in July, according to federal inflation data — though experts say it’s too soon to know how much of the drop, if any, can be attributed to Trump’s drug pricing deals. The site has relied on GoodRx’s pricing data and technology to power many of its listings and blends pre-existing discounts from drugmakers with newly negotiated prices.
At the Republican midterm convention last month , Trump said, “We went from the highest prescription drug prices, by far, anywhere in the world, to the lowest prescription drug prices anywhere in the world.”
A recent analysis from KFF finds that TrumpRx prices are competitive with prices in other countries for a small number of cancer and cholesterol medications. In many cases, Americans aren’t getting the best deals compared with the rest of the world.
Take Ozempic. For the average patient in the U.S. paying out of pocket, the blockbuster diabetes drug can cost $349 to more than $1,000 a month. It’s $349 through TrumpRx. Yet in several other wealthy countries, the next-highest price is $190 a month, according to KFF, a nonpartisan research group.
Enbrel is an even starker example. A monthly supply of the rheumatoid arthritis drug costs $3,354 through TrumpRx, more than five times the $641 average in the other countries where researchers found prices.
Some drugs, however, come out well ahead. Rydapt, a drug used to treat certain blood cancers, costs $2,909 for 56 capsules through TrumpRx — less than half the $5,901 price for the same amount in France, the next-cheapest country.
Those disparities run throughout the site, according to the KFF analysis. The report, which didn’t compare TrumpRx savings within the U.S., offers one of the first broad worldwide comparisons of Trump’s drug pricing claims.
The analysis looked at 32 brand-name drugs sold through TrumpRx that lacked generic or biosimilar equivalents. Researchers focused on those drugs because patients don’t have the option of switching to cheaper versions, meaning the discounts offered through TrumpRx could have a greater impact on what they pay.
The group compared the prices with those in 11 other wealthy countries, including Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom. The prices are current as of Aug. 26.
The results were almost evenly split. For 17 of the drugs, the TrumpRx prices were lower than the average prices abroad. For 15, they were higher. But Trump has promised Americans the lowest prices in the world. By that measure, the results were less favorable: Only five were actually the lowest-priced, while 13 were the highest-priced.
“It’s kind of a mixed bag,” said Juliette Cubanski, deputy director of the Medicare policy program at KFF, who co-authored the report. “Even with the reductions that may have been agreed to by manufacturers who are listing their drugs on the TrumpRx website, the prices that they’re offering, even at a discount, still continue to be higher than prices in comparable countries.”
The findings offer an early look at both the promise and the limits of Trump’s approach to lowering drug prices.
Americans routinely pay more for prescription drugs than patients in other wealthy countries, even when the medications are made by the same companies. The TrumpRx discounts, the White House says, stem from Trump’s “ most favored nation ” pricing deals, agreements with drugmakers to charge Americans the lower prices they offer other countries in exchange for tariff relief. But the discounts can vary widely, the analysis found, and they haven’t consistently produced the lowest prices Trump promised.
“I’m not surprised by these findings,” said Dr. Benjamin Rome, a primary care physician and health policy researcher at Harvard Medical School. “Any of us who have been following drug prices realized, as soon as TrumpRx was launched, it was a limited number of drugs and it was clear that the prices that were there were not always going to be linked or in any way related to what the prices are in other countries.”
It’s a markedly different approach from the one taken by Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden.
Rather than use Medicare’s power to negotiate prices for a limited number of costly drugs each year, TrumpRx relies largely on voluntary agreements with individual drugmakers to offer discounted prices directly to consumers. (The exact details of the agreements remain largely confidential, and the White House has declined to disclose them.)
TrumpRx doesn’t sell the drugs directly. For many drugs, it sends consumers to manufacturer programs through which they can obtain coupons or discounted cash prices without insurance.
That’s not how most people get their prescription drugs. About 9 in 10 Americans have some form of health insurance , meaning many pay for medications through private insurance, Medicare or Medicaid — although discounted cash-pay options have become increasingly popular as insurance has gotten more expensive. The money spent on TrumpRx doesn’t count toward a patient’s copay or deductible.
“They’re highly selected products where the manufacturer is willing to offer a discount,” Rome said. “Maybe they’re not the products causing the highest spending in the U.S. in some cases or are products where they were already offering confidential discounts, but now they’re making those discounts more public.”
The site now includes several cheaper, generic medications. “But those generics and the low prices for those generics pre-existed the TrumpRx website ,” Cubanski said.
The KFF analysis doesn’t capture every drug available through TrumpRx, and there are limits to how much can be concluded from it.
Antonio Ciaccia, CEO of 46brooklyn Research, a group that tracks drug pricing in the U.S., counts about 80 brand-name drugs currently on TrumpRx, while KFF was able to compare prices for 32.
Part of the challenge, Ciaccia said, is that some drugs sold in the U.S. aren’t available in all of the countries KFF examined. That can make direct comparisons difficult.
“One of the big differences is the U.S. market does have more products in it than international markets, so that is noteworthy to the extent we have options here in the U.S. rather than a one-size-fits-all treatment approach,” he said.
International prices aren’t always perfectly comparable, either, he said. The analysis relied on publicly available prices, which may not include confidential discounts negotiated between foreign governments and drugmakers.
Ciaccia also noted that KFF’s 11 comparison countries don’t exactly match the countries used in some of the administration’s international pricing programs.
A White House spokesperson referred NBC News to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services for comment. The CMS didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Those limitations don’t change the basic comparison at the heart of Trump’s claim: whether the prices offered to Americans match or beat those available abroad.
“We wanted to put that claim to the test with this analysis,” Cubanski said. “There is not a clear pattern across the board for higher prices or no consistent pattern across the board for lower prices. ”
And the administration has increasingly made broader claims that it has accomplished just that

articles.title_orig: This Is Not an Anniversary
articles.title_zh: This Is Not an Anniversary
articles.content_orig:
Does remembering the date of October 7 make it easier to name?
A man carries away a Palestinian killed in an Israeli airstrike at the Erez crossing between Israel and the northern Gaza Strip, on October 7, 2023.
The world remembers Gaza again this week. Had Palestinians wanted remembrance after each date we experienced atrocity, a full, long year wouldn’t have enough days. We have been faithful victims, though, haven’t we? Since 2023, the world has applauded the resilience of our bare chests standing up to the tanks grinding us dead. Our blood must’ve shed beautifully. The women and children mourning everything and everyone they had ever known have cried in perfect tears for protests and, indeed, outraged slogans. Our homes, no longer recognizable, could have been spared if they had not borne witness to lifetimes of destruction. And if only our screams hadn’t been too loud. Three years in, forgive us for not making as many stories about our sons and daughters as the world can give standing ovations. I wish my late journalist colleagues were a bit more courageous to commit a crime and call it out. They would have been worthy of support. Probably they would’ve been deserving of protection.
My life has become a tale of a thousand anniversaries. So I dare ask: Does remembering the date of a tragedy make it easier to name? To live with? How is recalling our trauma—and dedicating an anniversary for it—going to help erase it? How is the mere reflection on something still happening and painful beyond any human’s language will bring it to an end? The notion of marking an anniversary that kicked off a rather inhumane and unimaginable memory in a long history of erasure points to the fact that the world has already moved on. It supposes that all we ever asked for was empathy. And that, frankly, is why we’re more at peace with a senseless world than we are with our tragedies. If the moral urge behind holding an anniversary is to hold space for the grief that the past few years have inflicted, by no means should this say that we’re past the grieving. If it was to end this grief, then we’re not even in any way close to doing so.
And although I’ve written constantly and with abundant detail about all the personal and collective agony I have endured over the last three years, I still haven’t been able to put into words the true feeling of realizing that with each anniversary of death we become one year closer to life. But here is what I am able to say.
A day on which entire bloodlines were erased from the civil registry should not be an anniversary.
A day our mothers were crushed beneath the concrete of their own kitchens should not be an anniversary.
A day newborns suffocated in dark, unpowered incubators should not be an anniversary.
A day flour sacks were soaked in the blood of men standing in line for bread should not be an anniversary.
A day children had their limbs amputated without anesthesia on blood-slicked hospital floors should not be an anniversary.
A day thousands of tons of explosives flattened every school, university, hospital, and library should not be an anniversary.
A day our grandparents were forced to relive their displacement under relentless bombardment should not be an anniversary.
A day white shroud shortages forced us to bury three generations in a single shallow trench should not be an anniversary.
A day parents carried what remained of their children in plastic bags should not be an anniversary.
A day entire cities were turned into a blinding wasteland of pulverized stone and bone should not be an anniversary.
A day refugee tents were set ablaze while families slept on the sand should not be an anniversary.
A day doctors, poets, teachers, civil defense crews, and journalists were targeted for bearing witness should not be an anniversary.
A day mothers dug through scorching rubble with bare hands until their fingernails ripped away should not be an anniversary.
A day drop-delivered aid crushed the starving people it was meant to feed should not be an anniversary.
A day human beings were hunted through ruined alleyways by silent quadcopters should not be an anniversary.
A day ancient olive groves, centuries-old mosques and churches, and family photo albums were bulldozed into dirt should not be an anniversary.
A day an entire generation was orphaned, maimed, and stripped of a future should not be an anniversary.
A day hundreds of infants starved to death while their mothers did not have enough formula to feed them should not be an anniversary.
A day the sky turned into a screaming engine of death overhead should not be an anniversary.
A day our memories, our songs, and our homes were buried under mountains of gray ash should not be an anniversary.
A day the global audience watched a live-streamed genocide and called it defense should not be an anniversary.
Do not attempt to mark a date on a calendar that is not yours. If you do, keep your prayers—or celebrations—and let us keep what remains of your dignity.

articles.title_zh: 3 Golisano patients have measles; health officials push vaccines
articles.content_orig:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak, the first such declaration by a U.S. state since cases ​began surging in 2025.
The state also expanded the pool of health professionals ​allowed to administer measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccines as cases rise in rural communities.
New York has reported 108 measles cases this year through October 3, ​including 92 since July 15 in under-immunized rural communities across 18 counties, well above typical annual levels, according to the executive order.
Seven of the cases are in New York City and 101 ​are elsewhere in the state, the governor’s office said. Local health departments have administered ​more than 1,000 MMR doses in rural areas since July 15.
Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000. For the quarter century that followed, there were an average of just 180 measles cases per year nationwide, federal data shows.
But measles started to make an historic resurgence in 2025, and the outbreak in New York is far from the largest the US has seen in the past two years. There were at least 762 cases associated with an outbreak in West Texas last year, and an outbreak in South Carolina reached nearly 1,000 cases before it was declared over in April.
Neighboring Pennsylvania is battling a fast-spreading ‌outbreak, ⁠with 977 cases and five deaths as of October 2, mostly in rural counties that border New York, the order said.
Pennsylvania health officials said on Monday the state’s total had passed 1,000 cases, making it the largest state outbreak in more than ​three decades.
The US ​is having its ⁠worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The order ​allows registered nurses to order tests for suspected measles and pharmacists ​to vaccinate ⁠children as young as two. It also requires all MMR vaccinations to be reported to state or New York City immunization registries within 72 hours, while waiving adults’ ⁠consent for ​such reporting.
Vaccination itself still requires the consent of ​the patient or a legal guardian. The emergency took effect on Monday and runs through November 4.
Reuters contributed to this story.

articles.title_orig: Astronaut Christina Koch’s Eagles weekend was out of this world
articles.title_zh: Astronaut Christina Koch’s Eagles weekend was out of this world
articles.content_orig:
It's no secret that Eagles fans are a dedicated fanbase. However, only one can say that they have watched the team from space.
The Eagles celebrated Astronaut Christina Koch at Lincoln Financial Field as the Eagles' Honorary Captain during Sunday's game against the Rams. Known for circumnavigating the moon earlier this year with the Artemis II mission and crew, Koch also holds the world record for the longest time spent on the International Space Station in one deployment, with 328 straight days.
Even while orbiting 250 miles above the Earth's surface on the International Space Station, Koch would tune in for Eagles games.
"We have the ability to have an internet connection for personal things, crew choice things they call it. It's just a way to have things that can keep you entertained on the weekends and things that you love and remind you of home," Koch said. "I did marry into it. My husband (Robert) is a diehard, long-term Eagles fan since he was a kid. I resisted a little while mainly because I didn't know a lot about football ... now I'm all in and I've been sort of addicted ever since.
"If I didn't have time to watch them because they were at a different time where I couldn't make it, I would watch the reruns on the NFL Network or something like that. And it was just such a treat when I could share that with my husband and other people on Earth. It was a way of connecting through that and to just kick back and have a little bit of fun."
Astronaut (and Eagles fan) Christina Koch received a hero's welcome as an Honorary Captain against the Rams. After Sunday's game, the Artemis II crew member spent time with Eagles rookies, as well as science students from the Franklin Institute on Monday.

While Koch had been to Eagles games in-person before, she had never been to a home game at Lincoln Financial Field until Sunday. Not only did she join the Eagles Captains for the coin toss, Koch also led nearly 70,000 fans in an E-A-G-L-E-S chant during the two-minute warning of the first half. The woman who â quite literally â had ventured out into where no human has been before, said she was scared to start the Eagles' fight song.
"It was amazing to be at this place I've heard so much about, a place I looked at from space where I knew that all these fans came together with how dedicated they are," Koch said. "Just to be surrounded by that energy, to be right next to the players on the field, to watch their focus, watch them practice, watch their preparation rituals, it was amazing. I'm completely honored to have that opportunity."
Of course, Koch herself is no stranger to performing under pressure. During her time at the International Space Station, she participated in the first-ever all-female spacewalk, watching continents fly by below her feet as the station traveled at 17,500 miles an hour. For the Artemis II mission, Koch and the other astronauts trained for nearly three years, preparing for every single scenario â everything that could go wrong.
Koch's visit to the Eagles organization was part of NASA's Inspiration Tour, following the success of the Artemis II mission where Koch and the rest of the crew orbited farther from earth than any humans before. As it turns out, one of the many inspired by Artemis II was an Eagles Cheerleader. Before Sunday's game, Megan McKeon, a second-year cheerleader, had the opportunity to tell Koch that the mission inspired her to pursue a master's degree in planetary sciences.
"That moment was probably one of the most memorable and amazing ones of the whole game because she took the time to share her story personally with me and I could tell how much it meant to her and it truly did make an actual difference in her life," Koch said.
"I've been hearing stories like that from a lot of different people, but to meet someone firsthand that could tell me that they took the inspiration that the mission gave them and did something with it was really amazing. That was really all we ever wanted as a crew, was for it to have a positive impact on people's lives."
Koch also met Saquon Barkley on Saturday while touring the Jefferson Health Training Complex. The All-Pro running back had heard Koch was in the Eagles facility and set out to find her.
"He was super into space and the mission," Koch said.
The day after the game, the record-breaking astronaut spent time with Eagles rookies, as well as science students from the Franklin Institute on Monday. After being part of the Eagles' gameday experience, Koch got to show the Eagles rookies a glimpse into her world, answering questions before exploring the exhibits at the institute.
"Truth be told, that team inspires me, how they come into the arena and do their jobs under all that enormous, enormous pressure," Koch said. "It's been a source of inspiration. So, to be able to see it firsthand was really special." - Written by Caroline Connor

articles.content_orig:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Two seaside resorts in New England are among the best on the planet, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
The travel publication released a list of the 50 best resorts in the world on Tuesday, part of its 39th Annual Readers’ Choice Awards , and Chatham Bars Inn in Chatham ranked No. 18. Weekapaug Inn in Westerly, R.I. ranked No. 28.
Chatham Bars Inn , which was also named the No. 1 resort in New England , is “a benchmark of luxury on the Cape,” Conde Nast Traveler wrote.
“If you’re looking for a full-service resort with all the bells and whistles and then some, this is it, including an eight-acre private farm to stock the resort’s numerous dining and drinking outlets; one of the better spas on the Cape; an expansive pool deck with F&B service; a private quarter-mile beachfront; tennis courts with lessons available; and a 24-hour gym,” wrote the publication.
Resort officials celebrated on social media , writing, “Thank you to our incredible team and to our guests and supporters who voted for us. We’re grateful to be recognized alongside so many remarkable destinations.”
Weekapaug Inn, also named the No. 2 resort in New England , is a historic getaway in Rhode Island.
“A recently renovated legendary seaside inn on the National Register of Historic Places, the 27-room, six-suite Weekapaug Inn is a three-hour drive from New York and less than two from Boston—ideal for a quick weekend jaunt,” wrote Conde Nast Traveler .
Visitors enjoy guided nature walks, golf, tennis, and boating expeditions in historic vessels, noted the publication.
Officials at Weekapaug Inn also shared their excitement on social media , writing, “Thank you to the Condé Nast Traveler readers who voted, and to our incredible teams for truly delivering the best of service, cuisine, and luxury, year after year. We hope to share our award-winning experiences with you soon.”
The No. 1 resort in the world is Cheval Blanc Seychelles, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
This year, Conde Nast Traveler readers cast 798,867 votes for the annual awards, determining the very best in hotels, resorts, spas, airlines, and more worldwide. The results will be featured in the magazine’s November issue.
Kristi Palma is the travel writer for Boston.com, focusing on the six New England states. She covers airlines, hotels, and things to do across Boston and New England. She is the author of the award-winning Scenic Six , a weekly travel newsletter.

articles.title_orig: Google's AI Detection Website Is Now Available
articles.title_zh: Google's AI Detection Website Is Now Available
articles.content_orig:
SynthID Detector will flag content created with AI tools from OpenAI, Google, Apple and other companies.
Google is making SynthID Detector, its web tool for identifying AI-created and AI-edited content, available to everyone . The web-based tool is able to flag images, video and audio clips created with AI tools from Google, OpenAI, NVIDIA and Kakao. It's free to use, but does require users to log in with a Google, OpenAI or Apple account.
The website will also be one of the first AI detection tools that will be able to identify images created with Apple's AI features, like Image Playground. Google says support for images created and edited with Apple Intelligence is coming "soon."
Google has been working on SynthID Detector for more than a year , and previously made versions of it available to journalists and other "media professionals." Now, anyone can visit synthid.com to check whether a piece of content has a SynthID watermark. The company has other methods for detecting SynthID watermarks and C2PA content credentials, including its " Circle to Search " feature and the Gemini app itself. But creating a dedicated website for detection makes these capabilities a bit easier to access, especially for people not already using Google's AI tools.
As with all AI detection features, there are some limitations. SynthID Detector can't detect all AI-generated content, since many companies rely on different standards for watermarking. Watermarks can also be stripped from content in some situations. And Google's website doesn't distinguish between content that was entirely AI-created and content that was merely edited with it. So it won't provide specific details about how a particular piece of content was created or which aspects might be synthetic.
While SynthID Detector is a step in the right direction, verifying AI-generated content is still far from foolproof. AI detection tools like SynthID Detector rely on a patchwork of different standards so there's no such thing as a universal checker. Meta, for example, has been experimenting with its own web tool , which can identify images created or edited with its latest Muse Image models, but not those from other companies or even its own prior models.
But it does seem likely Google will get more companies to sign on to SynthID over time, The company previously said that ElevenLabs had committed to adding support for the watermarks. On its website, Google notes that it's "continuously working on extending our partnerships to allow detecting more generated media."

articles.title_orig: Space station crew heads home as replacements settle in for 6-month tour of duty
articles.title_zh: Space station crew heads home as replacements settle in for 6-month tour of duty
articles.content_orig:
The four people departing the International Space Station strapped into their Crew Dragon capsule and undocked early Wednesday, setting up re-entry and splashdown Thursday off the coast of Southern California to close out a 237-day stay in orbit.
With Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway at the controls, flanked on their left by European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and on the right by cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, the Crew Dragon "Freedom" backed away from the space-facing port on the forward Harmony module at 8:05 a.m. Eastern Time.
Sailing 260 miles above Cuba and the Bahamas, the capsule executed an automated loop over the top of the lab complex and slowly dropped away behind, exiting the safety zones around the station.
"We just wanted to give an enormous thank you to all of the team, our friends and colleagues on board the International Space Station, everybody in Houston, everybody at SpaceX, all around the world, with all of our international partners," Meir radioed as the Crew Dragon departed. "We have had the most incredible of expeditions ... and we will never forget it, and never forget all of your hard work."
After enjoying a final day in weightlessness, Meir and Hathaway will monitor a nine-minute and 20-second firing of the Crew Dragon's forward Draco thrusters starting at 10:46 a.m. ET on Thursday, setting up a fiery plunge back to Earth and splashdown off the coast of California at 11:34 a.m. ET.
Left behind aboard the space station were the Crew 13 fliers that replaced them — commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov — who were launched to the station on Oct. 1.
Also on board are Soyuz MS-29 commander Pyotr Dubrov, cosmonaut Anna Kikina and NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on July 14. They plan to remain aboard the station for eight months while Crew 13 is planning a six-month tour of duty.
In a brief ceremony Sunday, Meir turned command of the station over to Dubrov, saying Crew 12's departure would mark a "bittersweet" moment.
"We will be leaving our friends," she said. "But we know that we are going home to our friends, to our families, to all of our team members on the ground. So it's a lot of mixed, swirling emotions for all of us when one leaves a home like this up on the space station."
She presented a symbolic "key to the space station" to Dubrov, who said "it's a great honor and a great responsibility to be the commander of such a magnificent place like International Space Station."
"It has a special meaning for me today, because 69 years ago on this day (Oct. 4) the first Sputnik was launched. Today is the dawn of the space era for humanity, and International Space Station is the greatest symbol of what we can do if we work together."
The combined crews then gathered in a group hug, or "huggle," as Meir described it, forming a circle with arms around each other's shoulders.
With splashdown Thursday, Meir, Hathaway, Adenot and Fedyaev will wrap up a 237-day and five-hour mission, flying around the planet 3,792 times and logging nearly 101 million miles from start to finish.
Meir, wrapping up her second flight to the space station, will have logged a total of 442 days in space, completing four spacewalks during the Crew 12 mission and three during an earlier stay. Adenot carried out three back-to-back spacewalks of her own, including one with Meir and two with Menon.
