articles.title_orig: 11 Places to See the World's Most Magnificent Wildlife Migrations
articles.title_zh: 11 Places to See the World's Most Magnificent Wildlife Migrations
articles.content_orig:
Seeing an immense number  of creatures assembled in one place is a phenomenon worth travelling for. Here’s when, where and how to experience some of nature’s wildest gatherings.
Seeing any animal in the wild is a privilege — but seeing huge numbers is something else. For a start, it’s both humbling and heartening to encounter any species in abundance. It’s also genuinely exciting. When big groups of creatures seasonally cluster in one place, there’s always something to watch — from courting and mating to fighting or family-raising. It may be a sensory assault, too: noise, tumult, pungent smells, crashing waters, mad flurries of dust. And where masses gather to move together, hungry predators may lurk, adding a macabre but fascinating dimension. Here, we’ve picked the most dramatic migrations through the year and around the globe.
When to go: December to March
How does an insect the weight of a paperclip make a journey of 3,000 miles? That’s the feat of the extraordinary monarch butterfly, which somehow flutters from its summer breeding grounds — spread across Canada and the American northeast — to a patch of oyamel fir forest in the highlands west of Mexico City. Most only survive for a month or so but, in autumn, a generation emerges that lives eight times as long, capable of making this perilous trip. How they know where to go is a mystery — the butterflies that migrate are the great-great-grandchildren of those that left Mexico the previous spring. No matter, the results are spectacular: millions upon millions of orange-black wings blanketing trees, raining like tickertape. The Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, in the mountains of Michoacán state, is home to more than half of the overwintering colonies of the monarch butterfly’s eastern population. The sanctuary of El Rosario is easiest to reach; lesser-visited Sierra Chincua can be explored on horseback. The colourful, cobblestoned Mineral de Angangueo makes a good base.
The Indigenous Sámi of Europe’s far north work to their own calendar. Their year has eight seasons, and giđđa (spring) means melting snows, fast-increasing daylight and reindeer on the move: around April, the animals start migrating from their inland pastures towards the coast for summer grazing. Norway has around 275,000 reindeer, some wild, but mostly semi-domesticated herds that are ushered across the country’s Arctic plateaus by Sámi families whose livelihoods have depended on the practice for generations. Finnmarksvidda, an empty vastness of low hills, glacial lakes, pine barrens, birch woods and bogs in northernmost Norway, is a Sámi stronghold, where a few operators offer the chance to join the herders on the move. Days are shaped by the reindeer and the weather, perhaps involving sledding, snowmobiling or feeding the animals, followed by sharing stories around the fire, feasting on Arctic fish and sleeping in lavvus (traditional tents). Seeing swathes of animals trot across the tundra is a treat; being immersed in Sámi culture is an even greater privilege.
A strange thing happens off the South African coast each winter in the Southern Hemisphere: sardines in their millions, maybe billions, swarm north from Cape Agulhas, following a cold current towards the Indian Ocean. Strange, because it doesn’t benefit the sardines at all. But it’s a bumper buffet for other creatures: dolphins, tuna, seals, sharks, orcas and whales, plus dive-bombing cormorants, gannets and gulls. The result is marine mayhem. The sardines become silvery shape-shifting bait balls, chased down by great gangs of hungry predators and pierced by an avian invasion from above. Fish numbers have plunged in recent decades and the Sardine Run has become less predictable, but it’s still known as one of Earth’s greatest shoals. Activity peaks off Eastern Cape province, with boat trips leaving from towns such as Port St Johns and Gqeberha (formerly Port Elizabeth, handy for Addo Elephant National Park, too). Diving amid this chaos is thrilling, if challenging; snorkellers can launch into the action more quickly. Or, stay on board to watch the feasting frenzy from above.
With their massive bills and bodies, capacious pouches and wide, powerful wings, pelicans look both immensely impressive and distinctly prehistoric. Come spring, around 32,000 of them — mostly great whites, plus a significant scoop of dalmatians, the biggest species — leave their winter hangouts and make for Europe’s largest natural wetland, the Danube Delta. This splurge of rivers, lakes, marshes, forest, sandbars and reedbeds spreads mostly across eastern Romania. It’s a paradise for the pelicans, as well as other birds such as herons, storks and white-tailed eagles. The pelicans begin arriving in March, but May is an ideal time to visit, when colonies are a-bustle, large pods gather for herd-fishing and adults are in full breeding splendour, their great gular pouches beaming bright-orange. June, on the other hand, is good for spying chicks, and July the time to go for sheer numbers. Navigate the delta on boat trips with licensed guides (mandatory for exploring core areas) or stay on a floating hotel for 24/7 avian action.
When to go: July to October
No migration is easy, but the journey of the Pacific Northwest salmon reads like a Greek tragedy. Born in fresh water, they head out to sea, mature for a few years, then navigate back to their natal streams using the earth’s magnetic fields and their own sense of smell. They battle against the flow, leaping rapids, dodging grizzlies and eagles, only to spawn — and then die. It’s a privilege to witness this fatal journey, either from the riverbank, as the fish fling themselves from the froth, or in the water amid the shoals. The town of Campbell River, on Vancouver Island’s east coast, is the self-proclaimed ‘salmon capital of the world’, and the top spot for snorkelling with the chinook, coho, chum, pink and sockeye fighting to return home. Floating in the swift current, you might see hundreds, even thousands, of salmon swim past — and possibly some bears hanging about. From the banks, you can watch salmon leaping two metres into the air, perhaps only to be snatched by those waiting bears. From mid-August to late October, the Homalco First Nation run bear-watching trips to Bute Inlet.
When to go: October to December
The wildebeest in Kenya and Tanzania might grab the headlines, but the world’s biggest mammal migration happens further south. Kasanka National Park is one of Zambia’s smallest and, come October, around 10 million straw-coloured fruit bats overwhelm the remote enclave. By day, they weigh down the trees, wrapped snugly amid  the leaves. But at dusk they take flight, creating a deafening, whirling maelstrom of leathery wings as they seek supper — the bats weigh around 250g and can consume the same in fruit every night. At dawn they return, the maelstrom in reverse.  A good 10-hour drive from the capital of Lusaka, Kasanka National Park is offbeat, but tree hides and viewing platforms ensure the safari-goers who do make the effort get front-row seats. And it isn’t just bats: 114 mammal species have been recorded, from elephant to sitatunga antelope, plus 450 bird species. A trip here combines well with relatively nearby South Luangwa National Park, home to prolific wildlife and pioneering walking safaris.
When to go: June to October
Sea turtles: so cumbersome on land, so graceful underwater. These reptiles swim vast distances across oceans but must return to shore — back to the beach where they were born — to nest. There are seven species worldwide, five have nesting grounds in Costa Rica. Unsurprisingly, given its name is derived from ‘ tortuga ’ — the Spanish word for ‘turtle’ — Tortuguero is a hotspot. This national park on the country’s Caribbean coast is home to the western hemisphere’s largest green turtle rookery, as well as significant populations of leatherbacks and hawksbills.

articles.title_orig: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.title_zh: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.content_orig:
For scientists searching for life beyond Earth, rocky planets with atmospheres are among the most promising places to investigate. An atmosphere is essential for maintaining liquid water on a planet's surface. Yet among the more than 6,300 exoplanets cataloged thus far, most are not rocky, and only a small number of known rocky planets appear to possess atmospheres.
Now, researchers have added another world to that short list. In a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , a team led by University of Chicago scientist Brandon Park Coy reports evidence of an atmosphere surrounding HD 3167 b, a rocky super-Earth located 154 light-years away in the constellation Pisces. The intensely hot planet, classified as a "lava world," completes an orbit around its star in only one Earth day.
"What's so surprising is that the closer a rocky planet orbits its star, the harder it should be to have an atmosphere, because it's bombarded by stellar wind and gets more high-energy photons from the star. But it seems that many of these lava worlds do," explained Edwin Kite, UChicago associate professor of geophysical sciences and co-author of the study. "These planets are too hot for life, but by studying them, we can say something about the processes that matter for other rocky worlds."
In the Q&A below,Coy, a graduate student in Kite's group and first author on the study, explains why atmospheres on lava worlds are scientifically valuable, how researchers detected evidence for this one, and what they hope to learn next.
What was the goal of the survey that found this atmosphere-bearing exoplanet?
One of the driving questions that the James Webb Space Telescope is being used to answer is whether planets orbiting stars much smaller than the sun have atmospheres. It appears that most of those terrestrial planets don't -- they're just bare rock.
But surprisingly, we've found evidence that the majority of lava worlds -- similar in composition to Earth and Venus but much, much hotter -- might have atmospheres. Five terrestrial planets found with atmospheres, including the one described in this study, have been ultra-hot.
This planet, however, is the coldest lava world found so far with evidence of an atmosphere. This is interesting because we're trying to understand the temperature transition between planets with and without atmospheres.
The result is the first from a program led by Megan Weiner Mansfield, PhD'21, who's now at the University of Maryland. The goal of the program, which is looking at 10 ultra-hot lava worlds, is to see if there's a critical temperature over which you start seeing planets with atmospheres.
"We're interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world." -- Study author Brandon Park Coy
How can you tell if an exoplanet has an atmosphere?
Right now, directly looking at Earth-like planets for signs of life is out of reach. Instead, we can use the Webb telescope to detect light in the mid-infrared wavelength range to estimate the temperature of exoplanets, which can tell us if they might have atmospheres.
There are two primary ways that we study exoplanets. One is called transit, when the planet goes in front of the host star. Another called secondary eclipse, which is the method we used for this study, is when the planet passes behind its star, and we can measure how much light is lost. That difference tells us how much mid-infrared light comes from the planet itself, which essentially tells us how hot the planet is.
If a planet doesn't have an atmosphere, its star-facing, day side should be as hot as theoretically possible based on how reflective its surface is and its distance from the star. But an atmosphere would help redistribute heat from the day side to the night side. We see this happen on Venus -- there's almost no difference in surface temperature between the day and night sides, or between the poles and the equator. If a planet has an atmosphere, it might also have clouds that reflect incoming starlight and cool the dayside. So if a planet's day side is cooler than the maximum possible, it likely has an atmosphere.
The subject of this study, HD 3167 b, is noticeably cooler than its expected maximum, providing strong evidence that it has an atmosphere.
What do you think HD 3167 b's atmosphere is made of?
These lava worlds are so-named because the surface facing their star is likely melted rock. We think that HD 3167 b might have a silicate-rich composition, with a similar mixture of minerals that make up Earth's mantle. Before this study, we expected that any atmosphere on these ultra-hot planets would be composed of vaporized rock, but we're starting to see evidence that some might have heavier gases like carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, or water in their atmospheres.
The makeup of HD 3167 b's atmosphere is still up in the air. That's one reason we're so interested in getting new observations.
Why is this result important?
Because the four other lava worlds found to have atmospheres are in the ultra-hot regime, it raises questions about whether there's a critical transition temperature when silicate atmospheres start becoming very thick. Is there a temperature where these planets form silicate cloud decks that might reflect incoming radiation to space and cool its day side? This relatively cooler planet helps us better characterize and nail down this transition.
Despite how inhospitable they are for life, we're also interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world. We think that very early in the solar system's history, when the terrestrial planets formed, they were extremely hot due to the energy from all of the planetesimal collisions. Earth had what's known as a magma ocean stage with an entirely liquid surface. This result gives us a window into studying what conditions may have been like in Earth's first couple of million years.

articles.title_orig: Bigger than Manhattan: The record-breaking airport megahub that conquered the world
articles.title_zh: Bigger than Manhattan: The record-breaking airport megahub that conquered the world
articles.content_orig:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This CNN Travel series is, or was, sponsored by the country it highlights. CNN retains full editorial control over subject matter, reporting and frequency of the articles and videos within the sponsorship, in compliance with our policy .
Standing at the crossroad of continents, Istanbul has long been a global linchpin.
As Byzantium and then Constantinople, it controlled trade routes along the Silk Road and maritime passage from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean.
In the golden age of railways, Istanbul was the end point of the Orient Express, at the very cusp of Europe and Asia.
Now, in the 21st century, iGA Istanbul Airport is ruling the skies, having just overtaken London Heathrow as the best-connected airport on the planet.
“They’ve finally got the number one position,” says John Grant, chief analyst at OAG, a global travel data provider which has just released its Megahubs 2026 Index, comparing the world’s top airports.
The rankings are generated by comparing the number of scheduled connections to and from international flights , with the number of destinations served from the airport. They do this through a snapshot look at the busiest day of the year, which this year was August 2.
Gaining the top spot is “an important achievement for iGA Istanbul Airport and reflects the position we have built as a global aviation hub,” airport CEO Selahattin Bilgen tells CNN. “Today, we already serve approximately 350 destinations around the world, with significant room to grow further.”
Amsterdam Airport Schiphol is third place in this year’s ranking, followed by Kuala Lumpur at No.4 and Chicago O’Hare at No.5.
It’s been a swift and impressive rise for the award-winning $12 billion Istanbul Airport, which opened to much fanfare in 2018, about 20 miles outside Istanbul on the European side. This is a hub built for scale: Its huge 1.4-million-square-meter terminal is the world’s largest under one roof and the whole 76.5-million-square-meter site is bigger than Manhattan.
More than 84 million passengers pass through each year, making it the eighth busiest airport in the world. However, the long-term plan is to increase capacity to 200 million passengers per year, which is double the annual number currently handled by Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta, the world’s busiest airport.
“They’re going to be unassailable in the coming years,” says Grant. “They’ve got runway capacity. They’ve got a national airline that is hugely successful and continues to grow with new fleet orders. They’re very close to some of the most emergent markets in the world, such as Central Asia. They’ve benefited partly from the Middle East situation. They’re just very well placed.”
Istanbul Airport opened its fourth main runway last month and the end goal is for the hub to have nine: six main and three reserve.
The new  2,820-meter-long runway is its first to run east to west, meaning a reduction in taxiing and airborne times for westbound aircraft, saving time and fuel.
“They’re the only airport in the world that is licensed for three simultaneous runway operations,” says Grant, “You can build more frequency at those peak hours, and it gives you more operational flexibility. If you’ve got three runways, then you’re likely to improve your punctuality.”
Secrets of the sultan’s palace where concubines and eunuchs lived
Turkish Airlines has an 80% share of flights at Istanbul Airport and plays a key role in the hub’s success. Two years ago, it entered Guinness World Records for its achievement in flying to more countries than any other airline: 130 in total, as of 2026.
It operates a modern and rapidly expanding fleet of more than 500 Boeing and Airbus aircraft, including a diverse mix of narrow and widebody planes.
A younger fleet makes “a better impression” on customers, says Viktoriia Myroniuk, a senior lecturer in air transport management at the UK’s Cranfield University, reflecting on the polished service that helped earn Turkish Airlines its recent Skytrax award for Best Airline in Europe .
Newer aircraft are also more efficient, which, in this time of rising fuel prices, gives the airline a competitive edge, allowing them to lower ticket prices.
Selahattin Bilgen, CEO of iGA Istanbul Airport, tells CNN, “The efficiency and cost advantages we provide continue to attract new airlines to our network each year, and today we are one of only two major hubs worldwide serving the largest number of airlines.”
Infrastructure is equally key to that connectivity. “As a relatively new airport, iGA İstanbul Airport was designed from the outset with growth in mind, providing the capacity and flexibility to accommodate increasing passenger demand and support our role as a major international transfer hub.”
OAG’s 2026 Megahub rankings are inevitably affected by the ongoing disruption in the Middle East, as well as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
While other airports and regions have suffered, Istanbul Airport and Turkey’s geographical position and diplomatic relations have by chance granted it better fortune.
Istanbul Airport has the flexibility and capacity for growth that its competitors in the region lack. London Heathrow’s plan for a third runway remains highly controversial, due to the environmental impact in a highly built-up corner of southeast England. Amsterdam Schiphol, the world’s third best connected, has a flight cap of 488,000 movements a year.
“The fact that Istanbul Airport is slightly on the outskirts” means “they can operate 24/7,” says Myroniuk.
She also praises Turkish Airlines’ stopover program , which allows connecting passengers to take a break to explore Istanbul and enjoy free accommodation in partner hotels.
“I’m one of those unlucky passengers who really can’t sleep on board” and struggle on economy flights, Myroniuk says, but “your luggage stays with Turkish Airlines. You go to the perfect night’s rest.”
She married her brother, then he died. The monument to her grief was a Wonder of the Ancient World
It’s a form of sustainable tourism, she says, allowing travelers to embrace slower travel and to connect with local culture, rather than notching up cheap connecting flights with no experiences to show for it.
For many passengers it is also easier to get a visa to stop off in Turkey than it would be to take an exploratory tour from an EU airport, so that’s another advantage Istanbul Airport enjoys.
Although it’s hard to make any predictions in these turbulent times, Grant says that “all things being equal,” Istanbul will continue to hold onto its position in 2027.
“I think we’re going to see over the next three or four years the Chinese airports strengthen in their positions. We’re seeing more international growth from Chinese airlines, and that will help them,” he says.
International airlines including British Airways have yet to resume flying to the Middle East, but airports in the region will hopefully “get back to where they were,” says Grant. “All of which will continue to chip away at the position at Heathrow and Amsterdam Schiphol, and Paris, where we have European airports” that are reaching capacity.

articles.title_orig: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
articles.title_zh: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE — The technology that investors and governments are counting on to lift the global economy is also adding pressure that threatens growth, the head of the International Monetary Fund said, urging policymakers to stop delaying painful choices on debt.
Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told the audience at a Wednesday event in Singapore that artificial intelligence is "rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy."
But the triple forces of AI advancement, soaring energy costs and record public debt are challenging the already "underwhelming" growth this decade.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here," Georgieva said.
Speaking ahead of a series of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that kick off next week, Georgieva framed the global economy as being tugged in two directions at once: a "negative energy supply shock" from the war in the Gulf, now in its eighth month, and a "positive demand shock" from the AI investment boom. The combined effect, she said, is "highly uneven across the world."
On the upside, global AI investment as a share of GDP will reach, and likely exceed, the amounts that went into building the railroads, electricity grid, or telecommunications network. AI hardware and related technology products already account for more than a tenth of world goods trade, she said.
The IMF estimates that AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual world growth if done right. "Going from 3% to 3.5% over a decade — that is like adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy," Georgieva said.
But the benefits are likely highly concentrated. The boom largely bypasses economies less involved in the global AI supply chain, "increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe," she said.
The boom also feeds the inflation worry that has dogged policymakers from the U.S. to Europe and Asia. "The AI building boom is inflationary," she said, as are energy and food shocks, tariffs and defense spending.
Oil prices have stayed above $100 per barrel as the Middle East conflict dragged on with few signs of a diplomatic off-ramp. Retail diesel prices also rose to record highs as refining capacity squeezed energy supplies.
That inflation pressure flows straight into bond markets, as bond yields in the U.S., Germany, and Japan have surged to their highest levels in decades . Ballooning long-term private bond issuance by AI-related borrowers also competes with governments for capital, although part of the rise may reflect expectations of faster growth, Georgieva said.
Global public debt is near its highest level since World War II and on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP, with advanced economies the "worst offenders," Georgieva said. For 17 years, governments had "a relatively easy ride" because interest rates stayed below growth rates. "Higher interest rates now put an end to that."
The interest-to-growth differential is now "much less favourable" and "set to climb higher," she said, which means the growth needed to reduce debt ratios without fiscal effort is now "out of reach in the near term."
The strain is already visible in Europe, where spreads over German bunds are widening not just for France and Italy but for Ireland, Portugal and others that had reduced debt and deficits after the euro-area crisis.
After a string of shocks that have ballooned public debt and most countries' fiscal deficits remained above pre-pandemic averages, "fiscal space is crying out for replenishment," Georgieva said.
Georgieva also pointed to a financial stability risk in the AI boom itself. Strong corporate earnings are driving share prices and wealth effects, she said, but "should earnings fall short, however, hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock."
Citing Amara's Law, which holds that people overestimate a new technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run, she said it is "somewhere in the transition between today's AI building boom and tomorrow's arrival of AI's benefits that we will traverse the period of maximum risk."
Georgieva said the first line of defense is regulation and supervision. "Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries' monetary policy," she said.

articles.title_zh: IceCube, high-energy neutrinos, and Francis Halzen win 2026’s Physics Nobel
articles.content_orig:
Credit : Bryce Richter / UW–Madison
An astrophysics column on big questions and our universe.
There’s a whole entire Universe out there, and the more we learn about it as it actually is, the greater our potential becomes to achieve great things as a civilization, even if the path from knowledge to improving humanity is far from clear. The Nobel Prize was set up more than 100 years ago with the express purpose of rewarding those whose work provides the “greatest benefit to humankind” in a number of disciplines, including physics. We couldn’t foresee that:
Similarly, we cannot know what advances will arise in the future from advances made today in fields like elementary particle physics, gravitational waves, or neutrino astronomy, but possibilities range from computational advances to superior timekeeping technologies to extraterrestrial communication. One thing is certain, however: we have to make the fundamental advance, first, if we ever hope to find out. In many ways, that’s what the science of physics is all about.
It’s for that reason that the world ought to be incredibly excited that the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics has gone to Francis Halzen , for “decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” which is a remarkable testament to what a single individual can accomplish with a creative idea, a lot of hard work and organization, persistence, a strong national investment in science, and quite a bit of good luck. Here’s the story of this remarkable advance in neutrino physics and astrophysics.
The idea of IceCube was born 39 years ago, back before “neutrino astrophysics” was a field that went beyond our Solar System. Prior to 1987, neutrino astrophysics was restricted solely to measuring the neutrinos coming from within the Solar System: by building a large tank of fluid deep underground. Starting in 1968 , the idea was that neutrinos from the Sun, occasionally, would interact with an atomic nucleus, transmuting a neutron into a proton, and converting the neutrino into an electron in the process. By looking for the newly transmuted nuclei, solar neutrinos could then be detected.
In principle, nuclear reactions would occur all across the Universe, releasing neutrinos when they did, but the flux would be far too low to detect them. However, due to contemporaneous interest in grand unified theories , particle physicists had begun building much larger tanks of fluid surrounded by photomultiplier tubes, with the idea being to detect any spontaneously decaying protons by measuring their faster-than-light in the liquid medium radiation: Cherenkov radiation .
The major experiment of the 1980s, Kamiokande , was originally an experiment to search for nucleon decay in Kamioka, Japan. Running for several years, it only obtained null results, until the day of February 24, 1987. All of a sudden, an array of signals emerged: 12 of them (antineutrinos, technically) in the Kamiokande II detector alone . Four hours later, the light arrived as well, confirming this was indeed a supernova event. Kamiokande, the Kamioka nucleon decay experiment, kept the same acronym, but renamed itself to the Kamioka neutrino detector experiment. From a failed search for proton decay , the science of neutrino astronomy was born.
Over the subsequent years and decades, most approaches to neutrino detection simply scaled up this approach. Large, underground, liquid-filled detectors lined with photomultiplier tubes optimized to detect Cherenkov radiation were the key to building neutrino detectors, including Super-Kamiokande and the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNOLab), where the original research led to a Nobel Prize awarded in 2002 for neutrino physics and the upgraded research led to one in 2015 for neutrino oscillations.
However, in the aftermath of the 1987 supernova and subsequent neutrino detection, Francis Halzen began thinking about a different approach. Giant tanks were fundamentally limited in a key way: the effective volume available for interactions with neutrinos was constrained to be no larger than the size of your tank. If you wanted to find rare events, your only options were to either build a larger tank or to wait for longer periods of time, until such a neutrino from a rare event happened to interact within your detector.
Halzen came up with an alternative in 1988, which he merely (and humbly) referred to as a “cute idea,” which was to do away with a photomultiplier tube-lined tank entirely. Instead, he wondered, given that there’s so much ice located at the Earth’s south pole, could one simply use Antarctic ice as the “detector” for interacting with neutrinos instead?
Of course, it wouldn’t be possible or practical to use the entire Antarctic ice sheet, but Halzen realized that if you restricted yourself to a mere section of it — a large, cubical block — you could vastly increase the potential interaction volume over what you could ever hope to build with a conventional, liquid-filled and photomultiplier tube-lined detector. If it could be implemented successfully, Halzen’s vision could bring about a neutrino detector that was able to see events that were far rarer than the other neutrino detector designs would be sensitive to.
We had a longstanding hint of this from cosmic rays: non-neutrino particles (mostly protons, but also some heavier nuclei) that struck and interacted with Earth’s upper atmosphere, producing energetic particle showers. Sometimes, the daughter particles emerging from the shower could be detected directly on the ground, but most frequently, the shower of particles would interact with the Earth’s atmosphere: moving faster-than-light in the medium of air, and producing a cone of blue light that was once again the hallmark of Cherenkov radiation. Arrays of Cherenkov telescopes routinely detect this light, and reconstruct the signatures (and energies) of the particles that originally created them. When they do, they find that there are cosmic particles out there far, far more energetic than anything we could ever hope to realistically produce in laboratory experiments here on Earth.
If these high-energy particles — albeit, rare particles — are out there in the Universe, ostensibly created by high-energy sources like neutron stars, black holes, and active quasars, then it stands to reason that similar processes will create ultra-energetic neutrinos as well. However, since the number of particles above a given energy rapidly decreases as a function of energy, it would also imply that ultra high-energy neutrino events should be exceedingly rare as well, requiring enormous volumes of “detector material” in order to even see one or a few of them.
Super-Kamiokande is the world’s largest operational neutrino detector tank, holding just over 50,000 tonnes of extraordinarily pure water, but is only about 40 meters on a side. (Technically, in a cylindrical shape.) For comparison, however, if you went deep into the Antarctic ice, you should be able to find ice that is:
Halzen’s idea was to use hot water to bore cylindrical holes straight down into the Antarctic ice at regularly spaced intervals, and then to place specialized Cherenkov detectors down deep within the ice itself, filling the gaps back up with water to restore the ice back to its pristine, block-like state. If these detectors were spaced out over a volume of ice that was a cubic kilometer in size — 1 km × 1 km × 1 km — it would possess 20,000 times the detection volume of Super-Kamiokande!
The prototype for what would become the IceCube neutrino detector was known as AMANDA: the Antarctic Muon And Neutrino Detector Array . AMANDA was made up of optical modules — each with one photomultiplier tube inside to be sensitive to Cherenkov light — that were sunk into the Antarctic ice beneath the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. articles.title_orig: World shares, euro slide as high oil prices, fiscal worries linger
articles.title_zh: World shares, euro slide as high oil prices, fiscal worries linger
articles.content_orig:
US financial markets have been whipsawed as bond market fears grow, pushing Treasury yields to their highest levels in more than 20 years, and oil prices continue to fluctuate, despite the Nasdaq and S&P 500 hitting record peaks.
Wall Street closed lower on Wednesday as oil prices rose then fell due to renewed concerns about disruption to Middle East supplies.
Stocks fell after closing at record highs in the previous session on Tuesday, with yields on US government bonds climbing to 24-year highs as investors worried about the impact of high oil prices on inflation and interest rates.
Oil prices initially climbed on Wednesday following a warning that Iran appeared to be stepping up attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, before closing lower after International Energy Agency (IEA) member states said they were ready to release more strategic reserves.
IEA member countries said they stand ready to release additional oil from their reserves if necessary and will prioritise diesel due to tight supplies of the fuel, the head of the organisation said on Wednesday.
G7 countries, in coordination with the IEA, agreed last Friday to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by fallout from the United States-Iran war.
The latest announcement from the IEA calmed oil markets after prices had climbed on Wednesday following a report from UK Maritime Trade Operations.
The maritime agency said on Tuesday that there had been nine attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and the Gulf combined.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, repeated Washington’s claims that it was in control of the strait and that oil flows were at close to normal levels.
Oil exports from the Gulf have recovered significantly in recent days, despite a surge in attacks on ships around the Strait of Hormuz, maritime experts and trackers say.
Gulf oil flows, excluding Iran, recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, while crude exports from the wider Middle East exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days during the month, maritime intelligence firm Kpler reported.
However, the recovery has come as attacks on tankers increase and shipping companies face higher freight, insurance and security costs.
On Tuesday, 12 crew members on a Panama-flagged tanker were injured in an attack by an unknown projectile while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement.

articles.title_zh: N.C. A&T Alumnus Featured in Netflix Reboot of “A Different World” - North Carolina Agricultural & Technical State University
articles.source: North Carolina Agricultural & Technical State University
articles.content_orig:
By Charity L. Cohen / 10/06/2026 Alumni , College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences
EAST GREENSBORO, N.C. (Oct. 6, 2026) – Forever a North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University Aggie and now a Hillman College Falcon, former Mister A&T Joshua Suiter ‘22 is starring in the Netflix reboot of the 1980s and 1990s hit sitcom “A Different World.”
The series, which debuted at No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S., has already been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original series, which helped shape national perceptions of historically Black college and university (HBCU) life and inspired generations of students.
Following a new generation of students at the iconic fictional HBCU, Hillman College, the sequel explores the lives of today’s students while examining the legacy of those who came before them. The series’ writing team includes Ashley Laverne Jackson, daughter of late civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘64.
Suiter portrays Andre, a fellow Hillman student alongside Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison). As Deborah begins her journey at Hillman, she works to establish her own identity beyond her parents’ legacy while experiencing the highs and challenges of campus life.
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered his calling for acting and musical theater at 7, quickly realizing that hours spent studying lines and practicing techniques felt like minutes. That passion led him to N.C. A&T, where he earned a B.F.A. in professional theatre from the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences.
While at A&T, Suiter built a strong foundation in the performing arts, gaining experience both on stage and behind the scenes. One of his notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” during the university’s first Town & Gown Gala in 2019, where he first met Guy, who reprises her role as Whitley in the reboot.
In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in the marketing and business aspects of performance and the entertainment industry. This versatility helped propel him into his professional career.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” said Suiter. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
As a talented and emerging actor who most recently appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” performing alongside prominent Hollywood actors, starring in “A Different World” represents a full-circle moment for Suiter as an HBCU alumnus, bringing him into a reimagined version of a series he grew up watching.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”
